passages.title: The disjointed letters and Zachariah's whispered prayer
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah Maryam opens with five letters whose meaning Allah has kept to Himself, and then, with no introduction at all, sets us down beside an old man praying under his breath. What holds ayat 1–6 together is the heading Allah places over the whole scene in ayah 2: this is **a reminder of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya**. Everything that follows — the hidden voice, the feeble bones, the fear for what would come after him, the request — is being shown to us as an episode of that mercy, named as mercy before we are told a single thing that happened.

## Letters withheld, mercy announced

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary on this sūrah not with grammar but with a memory. Muhammad bin Ishaq recorded a hadith of Umm Salamah in his *Sirah*, and Ahmad bin Hanbal recorded from Ibn Masʿud, the story of the Hijrah — the emigration — to Ethiopia from Makkah; the narration mentions that Jaʿfar bin Abi Talib recited the first part of this sūrah to An-Najashi and his companions. So the opening of Maryam is not only a passage that was revealed and read. It was carried out of Makkah by one of the emigrants and recited aloud.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note about where the sūrah sits in the muṣḥaf: Sūrah Maryam has been placed immediately after Sūrah Al-Kahf, presumably because there appears some kind of similarity between the two — the former dealing with unusual anecdotes, the latter also covering a number of extraordinary events. The reader is being moved from one set of wonders to another.

Then the first ayah: **كٓهيعٓصٓ** — *Kāf Hā Yā ʿAyn Ṣād*. Ibn Kathir does not re-open the subject here; he simply notes that the discussion about the separate letters has already preceded at the beginning of Sūrat Al-Baqarah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is blunter, and it is worth taking to heart: these are the letters known in Arabic as **ḥurūf muqaṭṭaʿah**, whose meanings are known only to Allah Taʿālā, and people should not even attempt to probe them.

That is not a dead end; it is a posture. The sūrah begins by placing something in front of you that you are told you cannot decode, and asks you to keep reading anyway. A believer's knowledge has an edge, and the very first ayah of this sūrah marks it.

And what comes immediately past that edge is not another puzzle but a name for what follows. **ذِكْرُ رَحْمَتِ رَبِّكَ عَبْدَهُ زَكَرِيَّا** — Ibn Kathir explains it plainly: this means that this is a reminder of Allah's mercy upon His servant Zakariyya. He also records that Yaḥyā bin Yaʿmar recited it *dhakkara raḥmata rabbika ʿabdahu Zakariyyā*, "He has reminded of your Lord's mercy to His servant Zakariyya," and notes that the name Zakariyya has been recited both with elongation and shortened, both recitations being well-known. Notice, too, how Allah names him: **ʿabdahu**, "His servant."

Who was he? Ibn Kathir says he was a great Prophet from the Prophets of the Children of Israel. And then a detail that changes the texture of the whole passage: in Sahih Al-Bukhari it is recorded that he was a carpenter, who used to eat from what he earned with his own hand through carpentry. A prophet of Allah, working wood for his bread. Hold that image — Ibn Kathir will use it later to settle an argument.

## The whisper, and what it carried

**إِذْ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُ نِدَاءً خَفِيًّا** — "when he called his Lord with a call in secret." Ibn Kathir answers the obvious question in one line: he only made his supplication secretly **because it is more beloved to Allah**. He then cites Qatādah on this ayah: "Verily, Allah knows the pious heart and He hears the hidden voice."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same lesson — that *nidāʾan khafiyyā* tells us it is better to beseech Allah in supplication in an undertone — and cites, through Qurṭubī, a narration from Sayyidnā Saʿd Ibn Abi Waqqāṣ that the Prophet ﷺ once said that surely the best way of making supplication to Allah is in an undertone, and the best sustenance is that which is sufficient for one's needs, neither more nor less than required.

Qatādah's words settle what could otherwise worry a person praying quietly: nothing is lost by lowering the voice. Allah knows the pious heart and hears the hidden voice. And so Zakariyya, peace be upon him — old, childless, and about to ask for something his own body ruled out — asks for it in a whisper.

What that whisper contained comes next. **قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي وَهَنَ الْعَظْمُ مِنِّي وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا** — "My Lord, my bones have grown feeble, and grey has flared up on my head."

*Wahana al-ʿaẓm*: Ibn Kathir glosses it as "I have become weak and feeble in strength." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up why the bones in particular are named: the human body becomes weak with the aging of the bones, because it is the bones that keep the body firm and upright; when the bones lose their strength, the whole body turns weak. He is not describing an ache. He is describing the failure of the frame that holds everything else up.

*Ishtaʿala*: its literal meaning, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is **a sudden burst of fire**; here the word is used as a simile for grey hair covering the head like a glow of fire. Ibn Kathir puts it from the other side — the grey hair has burned into the black hair — and adds that the intent is to inform of weakness and old age, and its external and internal traces. The image the commentaries hand us is not grey creeping slowly in. It is fire catching, and a whole head lit with it.

Then the turn: **وَلَمْ أَكُن بِدُعَائِكَ رَبِّ شَقِيًّا** — "and I have never been unblessed in my invocation to You, my Lord." Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is beautiful in its confidence: "I have not experienced from You except that You would respond to my supplication and that You would never refuse me in whatever I ask of You."

So in a single ayah he has said two things at once: *I am finished*, and *You have never once turned me away*. His weakness and his Lord's record of generosity are laid down in the same breath.

### Mentioning your need is part of the etiquette

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the ruling under exactly that heading: **mention of one's needs in supplication is desirable**. Zakariyya, peace be upon him, mentioned his weakness and old age — by referring to his bones — *before* making his supplication. Two reasons are given. First, in his peculiar circumstances of old age and physical weakness, it was not appropriate for him to be asking for a child. Second, the reason given by Imam Qurṭubī in his commentary: for the possible acceptance of a supplication, it is better to mention one's weakness, destitution and inadequacy. For this reason, Maʿārif adds, religious scholars have emphasised that one should recount Allah Taʿālā's blessings and his own exigency before making his supplication.

That is a whole method of duʿāʾ: *this is how frail I am; this is how generous You have always been; now here is what I need.*

And the need, when he names it, is not what a reader might assume. **وَإِنِّي خِفْتُ الْمَوَالِيَ مِن وَرَائِي وَكَانَتِ امْرَأَتِي عَاقِرًا** — "And verily I fear the *mawālī* after me, and my wife is barren."

*Mawālī* is the plural of *mawlā*, a word Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes has many meanings in Arabic — one of them a cousin, or other relations on the father's side, and that is the sense here. Ibn Kathir reports that Mujāhid, Qatādah and As-Suddī all said that in saying *mawālī*, Zakariyya meant his succeeding relatives.

And what did he fear from them? Ibn Kathir is explicit: the reason for his fear was that he was afraid **the generation that would succeed him would be a wicked generation**. So he asked Allah for a son who would be a Prophet after him, who would guide them with his prophethood and with what was revealed to him.

This is the hinge of the whole passage. His anxiety is not for a household or a family name — it is for religion outliving him. The translation before you captures it by supplying the missing word: "I am concerned about ˹the faith of˺ my relatives after me."

Then he names the second obstacle without flinching: *wa kānat imraʾatī ʿāqiran* — and my wife is barren. He does not soften the facts he is asking Allah to overturn. And only then comes the request: **فَهَبْ لِي مِن لَّدُنكَ وَلِيًّا** — "So give me from Yourself an heir." Having stated that the ordinary way is closed, on his side and on hers, he asks Allah for the gift *min ladunka*, from Himself.

## What kind of inheritance?

**يَرِثُنِي وَيَرِثُ مِنْ آلِ يَعْقُوبَ** — "who shall inherit me, and inherit also the posterity of Yaʿqūb."

This is the most heavily discussed clause in the passage, and both commentaries reach the same conclusion: the inheritance here is **prophethood and knowledge, not wealth**.

Ibn Kathir gives three arguments:

1. **It is beneath a prophet.** He was not afraid of them inheriting his wealth. A Prophet is too great in status and too lofty in esteem to become remorseful over his wealth in this fashion; he would not disdain to leave his wealth to his successive relatives and so ask for a son to receive his inheritance instead of them.
2. **He had no wealth to speak of.** Allah did not mention that Zakariyya was wealthy. On the contrary — here the carpenter's hands return — he was a carpenter who ate from the earnings of his own hand, and this type of person usually does not have a mass of wealth. Amassing wealth is not something normal for Prophets; they are the most abstentious in matters of this worldly life.
3. **The Sunnah restricts the meaning.** It is confirmed in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, in more than one narration, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"We (the Prophets) do not leave behind inheritance (of wealth). Whatever we leave behind, then it is charity."* And in a narration recorded by At-Tirmidhī with an authentic chain: *"We, Prophets, do not leave behind inheritance (of wealth)."* These hadiths, Ibn Kathir says, restrict Zakariyya's request to the inheritance of prophethood.

Ibn Kathir then adds an argument from the wording itself. Why the extra words "and inherit also the posterity of Yaʿqūb"? He compares Allah's statement *"And Sulaymān inherited from Dāwūd"* (27:16), which means that he inherited prophethood from him. Had wealth been meant, Sulaymān would not have been singled out with it among his brothers, and there would have been no important benefit in mentioning it at all — since it is already well-known and established in all the previous laws and divinely revealed creeds that the son inherits the wealth of his father. **If this was not referring to a specific type of inheritance, then Allah would not have mentioned it.**

Two early authorities are quoted on the same clause. Mujāhid said: "His inheritance was knowledge, and Zakariyya was one of the descendants of Yaʿqūb." And Abu Ṣāliḥ — reported by Hushaym, who was informed by Ismāʿīl bin Abi Khālid — said: "He would be a Prophet like his forefathers were Prophets."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān arrives at the same place under the heading *The Legacy of Prophets cannot be inherited*, and states that the religious scholars are all agreed that inheritance here does not mean wealth, for three reasons: it has not been established that Zakariyya had much wealth, so the question of who would inherit it does not even arise; it is inconsistent with the exalted position of a prophet to concern himself with such matters; and there is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, unanimously accepted by all religious scholars, narrated by Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah and At-Tirmidhī — that **the knowledgeable scholars are the inheritors of the prophets**, because the prophets do not leave any material wealth; their legacy is knowledge, and whoever has acquired that knowledge has received great fortune. Maʿārif also cites the narration in Sahih Al-Bukhari, through Sayyidah ʿĀʼishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "No one inherits our — that is, the prophets' — wealth, because whatever wealth we leave behind is ṣadaqah, charity."

Maʿārif adds one further argument from the wording that is hard to answer: the addition of *"and inherit from the family of Yaʿqūb"* confirms that material inheritance is not implied, because Yaḥyā, peace be upon him, could not have inherited the material wealth of the family of Yaʿqūb — that could only be inherited by their near relations, and it is against the law of inheritance for distant relations to receive any part of it in the presence of close relatives. (Maʿārif notes in passing, via Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, that even *Al-Kāfī* of Al-Kulainī, the well-known book of the Shīʿah school, carries the report that Sulaymān was the heir of Dāwūd and that Muhammad ﷺ was the heir of Sulaymān — which quite obviously cannot mean material wealth, and so points to the same thing: the wisdom and knowledge which all the prophets of Allah possess.)

### The last word of the prayer

**وَاجْعَلْهُ رَبِّ رَضِيًّا** — "and make him, my Lord, one with whom You are well pleased." Having asked for a son, he does not stop at the son. Ibn Kathir explains the request: make him pleasing to You and to Your creation; love him, and make him beloved to Your creatures, in both his religion and his character.

That is where the passage leaves him, and it is the measure of the man. He is not asking for an heir who will merely exist. He is asking for one whom Allah loves, whom people love, and whose religion and character are both sound.

## Living it

Six ayat, and a working pattern for anyone who prays:

- **Lower your voice.** He whispered — because that is more beloved to Allah, and because Allah knows the pious heart and hears the hidden voice (Qatādah). The undertone is not weaker prayer; the sources call it better prayer.
- **Say what is wrong, honestly.** Feeble bones, a head gone grey, a wife who could not bear children. He lays out every closed door before asking for what lies past them.
- **Recall His past kindness.** "I have never been unblessed in my invocation to You." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that scholars stress recounting Allah's blessings, alongside your own need, before you ask.
- **Ask for the right thing.** His fear was that the generation succeeding him would be a wicked one — and so his request was for a son who would carry prophethood and guidance, not a name or an estate.
- **Ask for their character, not only their existence.** *Rabbi raḍiyyā* — pleasing to Allah and to His creation, beloved in religion and in character.
- **Know what you actually leave behind.** The prophets leave no dinar and no dirham; their legacy is knowledge, and the scholars are their heirs.

And over all of it, ayah 2 keeps its hand: this is *a reminder of the mercy of your Lord*. The whisper was heard.

passages.title: Glad tidings of John and the sign of silence
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath:** an old man's prayer for a son is answered while he stands at worship — with the child's name already chosen — and when he asks how such a thing can be, and then asks for a sign to steady his heart, Allah gives him one: three nights and their days in which his tongue is held back from people while his body stays sound.

These five ayat are one conversation. It opens with an announcement, is interrupted by an astonished question, is answered by something more astonishing still, and closes with the answer walking out of the prayer-place and becoming visible to a whole community. Nothing in it stands alone; each turn only makes sense as a reply to the turn before. So it is best read the way it was spoken — as a single exchange that moves from *a prayer answered* to *a prayer answered so completely that the man who made it had to be steadied*.

## A prayer answered before the acceptance is even mentioned

Ibn Kathir makes a fine observation about how the passage opens. The Qur'an does not first say "and We accepted his supplication." It simply begins: *"O Zakariyya! Verily, We give you the good news of a son, whose name will be Yahya. We have given that name to none before (him)."* As Ibn Kathir puts it, this statement implies what is not mentioned — that his supplication was answered. The response *is* the record of the acceptance.

He sets beside it the parallel telling in Surah Āl-ʿImrān, where Zakariyya (peace be upon him) prays, *"O my Lord! Grant me from You, a good offspring. You are indeed the All-Hearer of invocation,"* and then the angels call him *"while he was standing in prayer in the Mihrab,"* saying: *"Allah gives you glad tidings of Yahya, confirming (believing in) the word from Allah, noble, keeping away from sexual relations with women, a Prophet, from among the righteous"* (3:38–39).

Notice what is given and what was never asked for. Zakariyya asked for offspring. He is given a son, a name for that son, and a character reference for him before he is conceived. The gift outruns the request — and the closing phrase of the announcement, *lam najʿal lahu min qablu samiyyā*, presses that further still.

Everything there turns on one word, **samiyy** (سَمِيّ). Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains that it carries two senses.

**First sense: "person having the same name."** On this reading, no child before Yahya had ever been called Yahya. This is what Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd said, as reported by Ibn Kathir — "no one had this name before him" — and Ibn Jarir preferred this interpretation, may Allah have mercy upon him. Maʿārif adds that this fact also suggests he possessed certain special attributes which were not granted to anyone else before him.

**Second sense: "similar."** On this reading the ayah is not about the sound of the name but about the man: some of his attributes and situations were peculiar to him and not shared by any other prophet, and he was unique in possessing them. Maʿārif gives as its example his self-abnegation and denial of worldly comforts — **ḥaṣūr** (حصور), the same word rendered in the Āl-ʿImrān passage quoted above as "keeping away from sexual relations with women."

**An important qualification.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, citing Mazharī, is careful to close off an overreach: it does not necessarily follow that Yahya was superior to all the prophets who preceded him, for the superiority over him of Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm Khalīlullāh and Sayyidnā Mūsā Kalīmullāh (peace be upon them both) is established and well known. A believer can honour what is distinctive in one servant of Allah without turning distinctiveness into a ranking.

## "How?" — and an answer that reaches further back than the question

The announcement lands on a man who cannot see a route from it to reality. *"My Lord! How can I have a son, when my wife is barren, and I have reached the extreme old age."*

Ibn Kathir is unusually vivid here. Zakariyya, he says, was amazed when his supplication was answered and he was given the good news of a son; he became extremely overjoyed, and asked how this child would be born to him and in what manner he would come. The wonder had solid grounds: his wife was an old woman who was barren and had not given birth to any children in her entire life. And Ibn Kathir states the husband's condition without euphemism — Zakariyya himself had become old and advanced in years, his bones had become feeble and thin, and "he had no potent semen or vigor for sexual intercourse."

The Arabic for that state of age is **ʿitiyyā** (عِتِيًّا). Maʿārif ul Qurʾān traces it to a root meaning *unresponsive* or *insensitive*, and says that in the present context it means the **dryness of the bones**. It is a far more physical word than "old age." Zakariyya is not reciting a number of years; he is describing a body that has stopped cooperating.

Read this way, the question is not doubt. It is a man looking at two dead ends — a barren wife and a dried-out body — and asking, in wonder rather than objection, by what route the promise will travel.

The reply comes, Ibn Kathir specifies, from **the angel**, in response to Zakariyya and his amazement. And two clauses do the work.

**"Thus says your Lord."** Ibn Kathir reads *kadhālika* (كَذَٰلِكَ) as closing the door on the obvious workaround: it means the birth of the son will be from *you* and from *this wife of yours* and not from any other woman. The two impossibilities Zakariyya named are not going to be bypassed. They are going to be the very material of the miracle.

**"It is easy for Me."** Ibn Kathir's gloss on **hayyin** (هَيِّن) is deliberately flat: it means simple and easy for Allah to do. What strains a body of feeble bones past breaking is, for the One who made that body, simply easy.

Then the angel does more than reassure. Ibn Kathir notes that he mentions to Zakariyya *that which is more amazing than what he was asking about*: *"Certainly I have created you before, when you had been nothing!"* Zakariyya's difficulty was getting from *a body with nothing left in it* to *a child*. But Allah had already brought him from *nothing at all* to *Zakariyya*. Ibn Kathir places beside it Allah's statement, *"Has there not been over man a period of time, when he was not a thing worth mentioning?"* (76:1). The argument is complete: whoever is astonished at creation from weakness has forgotten creation from nothing — and he is himself the standing proof of it.

## A sign asked for, a sign given, a sign carried out in public

The astonishment settles into a request: *"My Lord! Appoint for me a sign."* Ibn Kathir puts the request in Zakariyya's own register — *"Give me a sign and a proof of the existence of that which You have promised me, so that my soul will be at rest and my heart will be at ease with Your promise."* And he sets beside it Ibrāhīm's request (peace be upon him): *"My Lord! Show me how You give life to the dead." He (Allah) said: "Do you not believe?" He said: "Yes (I believe), but to put my heart at ease"* (2:260).

That parallel is the key to reading the request correctly. It is not for evidence to replace belief; it is for the settling of a heart that already believes. A believer can hold something as certain and still long to *feel* it as certain. Asking Allah for that steadiness is not a defect in faith — two prophets did it.

The sign granted is this: *"Your sign is that you shall not speak unto mankind for three nights, though having no bodily defect."*

The whole force of it hangs on **sawiyyā** (سَوِيًّا) — the word rendered above as "though having no bodily defect." Ibn Kathir's explanation of the clause is that "your tongue will be prevented from speaking for three nights while you are healthy and fit, without any sickness or illness." Maʿārif ul Qurʾān renders the word simply *healthy*, and explains why it had to be there: it denotes that Zakariyya's (peace be upon him) loss of speech for three days was **not** due to any illness, for during this entire period of three days he could utter words of prayer and supplication. That special condition was a miracle and a sign from Allah Taʿālā about his wife's pregnancy. Take the word away, and this is a sick old man who has lost his voice. Keep it, and this is a man in full health whose speech is withheld from people alone.

Ibn Kathir reports the same understanding from a wide field of the early authorities — **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Wahb, As-Suddī, Qatādah and others**: "His tongue was arrested without any sickness or illness." And **ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam** fills in the picture: "He used to recite and glorify Allah, but he was not able to speak to his people except by gestures."

**Where the reports differed.** Al-ʿAwfī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said of *three nights, though having no bodily defect*: "The nights were consecutive." Ibn Kathir notes the difference and judges that "the first statement that is reported from him and the majority is more correct" — that is, the reading of *sawiyyā* as sound and healthy.

**Three nights or three days?** Ibn Kathir resolves this by cross-reference to Surah Āl-ʿImrān: *"Your sign is that you shall not speak to mankind for three days except with signals. And remember your Lord much, and glorify (Him) in the afternoon and in the morning"* (3:41). Our passage says three *nights*; that ayah says three *days*. Ibn Kathir takes the pair as proof that he did not speak to his people for these three nights and their days as well — a full three-day stretch. And the words rendered "except with signals" — *illā ramzā* — mean, he explains, bodily gestures.

Which is exactly what happens next: *"Then he came out to his people from the Mihrab and he indicated to them by signs to glorify [Allah] in the morning and in the afternoon."*

Ibn Kathir identifies the place precisely: the **miḥrāb** he emerges from is the place where he was given the good news of the child. The prayer, the answer and the sign all belong to one spot — the place of his worship, where the angels had called him as he stood praying. He walks out of it carrying a public sign.

**"Fa-awḥā ilayhim" (فَأَوْحَىٰ إِلَيْهِمْ) — "he indicated to them by signs."** Ibn Kathir explains that he made a gesture to them that was **subtle and swift**. **Mujāhid** said simply, "He made a gesture," and **Wahb and Qatādah** said the same. The man who could not shape a word to his people could still, with a movement of his hand, give them a command.

**And what was the command?** Not "congratulate me." Not even "a child is coming." It was *sabbiḥū bukratan wa ʿashiyyā* (أَن سَبِّحُوا بُكْرَةً وَعَشِيًّا) — **glorify Allah in the morning and in the afternoon.** Ibn Kathir explains the purpose: that they should be agreeable to what he was commanded to do during these three days, to increase in his deeds and gratitude to Allah for what He had given him.

That is the quiet climax of the passage. A prophet receives the most personal gift of his life, is given a sign so unusual that it holds back his speech, and the first thing he does with the sign is turn his community toward glorifying Allah.

## Living it

**Ask, and ask for the impossible.** Ibn Kathir frames the opening ayah as a supplication answered without the acceptance even needing to be announced. Zakariyya prayed against barrenness and dried bones and was answered — and the answer came, in the Āl-ʿImrān telling, while he was standing in prayer in the miḥrāb.

**Measure your difficulty against the right yardstick.** The angel's reply does not argue that Zakariyya's case is less hard than it looks. It says the ease belongs to Allah, and then points to something more amazing than what he was asking about, already accomplished in his own person: *"Certainly I have created you before, when you had been nothing!"* Whatever seems closed to you, you are yourself evidence of a Creator who works from nothing.

**Wanting your heart settled is not weakness.** Zakariyya asked for a sign so that his soul would be at rest and his heart at ease, as Ibrāhīm asked to see the dead revived and said, "Yes (I believe), but to put my heart at ease." Belief and the longing for reassurance can live in the same chest.

**Let the gift produce worship, not just relief.** Zakariyya's three silent days were spent, on the report of ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam, reciting and glorifying Allah — and his one available gesture to his people was a call to do the same, morning and afternoon. When something you prayed long for finally arrives, this passage shows what to do with the first hours: increase in deeds and in gratitude to Allah for what He has given, and pull others into it with you.

passages.title: John given wisdom, tenderness, and peace
passages.tafsir:
**In brief:** After the promise of a son to Zakariyya, these four ayat turn to the boy himself. A command comes — hold the Book with strength — and then his portrait is drawn: what Allah gave him, what he became because of it, and the peace that crowns him at the three most solitary moments of any human life.

What holds the passage together is a single movement: **gift, then character, then reward.** Ayah 12 is a command and a gift (the Book, and wisdom). Ayah 13 lists further gifts that became his nature (tenderness, purity, piety). Ayah 14 shows that nature turned outward, toward his parents. Ayah 15 is the greeting of peace over him. Nothing here is Yahya's achievement standing alone; every quality is traced back to its Giver.

## The birth that the Qur'an passes over

Notice what is missing. A son had been promised to Zakariyya. Then, without a word about the pregnancy or the birth, ayah 12 simply calls out: *"O Yahya!"*

Ibn Kathir draws attention to this. The passage, he says, "implies what is not mentioned, that this promised boy was born and he was Yahya." The Qur'an leaves out the obvious — a promise from Allah does not need its fulfilment narrated — and spends its words instead on what the boy was given and what he became.

## "Take the Book with strength" (ayah 12)

*Yā Yaḥyā khudhi'l-kitāba bi-quwwah.* The rendering before us frames it as speech directed to the son — "It was said to his son: O Yahya!" — and Ibn Kathir introduces the words as Allah's own address to him. The Book here, Ibn Kathir explains, is the Tawrah: the scripture "which they used to study among themselves," and the law by which "the Prophets who were sent to the Jews used to rule... as did the scholars and rabbis among them." So this is not a vague call to piety. It is a boy being handed the living law of his people and told to master it.

The striking word is *bi-quwwah*, "with strength". Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and demanding: **"Learn the Book with strength" — in other words, learn it well, with zeal and studious effort.**

Two things are worth sitting with here. First, scripture is not something you drift into. The verb is *khudh*, "take" — take hold of it — and the manner is *quwwah*, force, exertion, seriousness. Casual acquaintance with the Book is not what is being asked for. Second, the command comes as a form of honour. Ibn Kathir places it in the frame of Allah's favour: "Because of how Allah favored him and his parents, He says..." To be told to carry the Book is itself a gift, to the boy and to the parents who were given him.

## "And We gave him wisdom while yet a child"

*Wa ātaynāhu'l-ḥukma ṣabiyyan.* The word *ḥukm* is rendered "wisdom" — and Ibn Kathir unpacks it as a cluster rather than a single quality: **understanding, knowledge, fortitude, diligence, and zeal for good and the pursuit of good.** It is intellectual (understanding, knowledge) and moral (fortitude, diligence) and affective (zeal, eagerness) all at once. A person who knows what is right, has the steadiness to hold to it, and actually wants it.

The last word of the ayah is what makes it remarkable: *ṣabiyyan*, "while still a boy". Ibn Kathir stresses the point — "He was still young in age when Allah gave him this knowledge. This is the reason that Allah mentioned it." He adds: "He was blessed with these characteristics even though he was young." Allah is not merely reporting a fact about Yahya's education; He is naming a favour. The gift arrived before the years that normally produce it.

## Tenderness and purity — gifts, not merely traits (ayah 13)

*Wa ḥanānan min ladunnā wa zakāh.* Grammatically, Ibn Kathir says the apparent meaning is that *ḥanānan* hangs on the same verb as the previous ayah — "and We gave him wisdom while yet a child" — so the sentence reads: **"We gave him wisdom, compassion and purity."** That small grammatical observation carries real weight. A soft heart is easy to read as a personality trait, something you either happen to have or do not. Here it stands among the things Allah *gave*. Tenderness is bestowed.

**Ḥanān.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the literal sense: soft-heartedness, compassion, and mercy — qualities "specially granted to Sayyidna Yahya (peace be upon him)." Ibn Kathir's phrasing is warmer still: *ḥanān* "means the love for affection and tenderness (towards others)" — not merely being kind when kindness is called for, but having an appetite for it. The early authorities gathered around a single reading: Ibn ʿAbbas — in the report of ʿAli bin Abi Talhah — said it means "mercy from Us", and ʿIkrimah, Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak all said the same. Mujahid put it as "gentleness from His Lord upon him." Ibn Kathir's summary of the man himself follows: "he was a compassionate man, who was righteous."

Here is the balance the passage strikes. The boy commanded to seize the Book *with strength* is, in the very next breath, given softness. Strength in scripture and tenderness toward people are not rivals; in Yahya they were issued together, from one hand.

**"From Us" (*min ladunnā*).** This phrase is not decoration. Ad-Dahhak added a comment that sharpens it: this is "mercy that no one would be able to give except Us." And Qatadah drew out a second beneficiary: "With it, Allah had mercy upon Zakariyya." The son's tenderness was itself an act of mercy toward the father — the man promised an heir received a boy whose very disposition was gentle with him.

**Zakāh.** The word means purity — Ibn Kathir defines it as "purity from filth, wickedness and sins". The early commentators pushed it in a practical direction: Qatadah said *zakāh* means "the righteous deed", and Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj both explained that "the righteous deed is the pure (*Zakah*) deed" — that is, purity is not an inner mood but shows itself as clean action. Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas a third shade: *zakāh* here "means that he was a blessing." Purity that others benefit from.

**"And he was mindful of Allah" (*wa kāna taqiyyan*).** Ibn Kathir's gloss goes further than avoidance: he was "pure and had no inclination to do sins." Not a man permanently straining against desires he barely contained, but one whose wants themselves had been cleansed — which, in the flow of the ayah, is the fruit of the gifts just listed.

## Kind to his parents — and the two things he was not (ayah 14)

*Wa barran bi-wālidayhi wa lam yakun jabbāran ʿaṣiyyā.*

The order matters, and Ibn Kathir makes it the point of the ayah: "After Allah mentioned Yahya's obedience to his Lord and that Allah created him full of mercy, purity and piety, He attached to it his obedience to his parents and his good treatment of them." Devotion to Allah and devotion to parents are placed on one thread.

*(A reflection of my own, not part of Ibn Kathir's comment: if the Qur'an binds these two together this tightly, then the home is where a person's religion is first put to the test — long before anywhere more public.)*

The two renderings before us are worth holding side by side: "kind to his parents" and "dutiful to his parents". One carries the warmth, the other the obligation; the ayah asks for both. Ibn Kathir specifies how far it reached: Yahya "refrained from disobeying them in speech, actions, commands and prohibitions." Four fronts. Not only doing what they asked, but not answering back; not only obeying the "do", but honouring the "don't".

Then the ayah closes with two negations: he was neither *jabbār*, arrogant, nor *ʿaṣiyy*, disobedient. Ibn Kathir reads this as flowing from what precedes — after describing that fourfold refusal to disobey them, he says, "Due to this Allah says, (and he was not arrogant or disobedient)."

The pairing is instructive, and here I am reflecting rather than reporting: disobedience toward parents rarely begins as disobedience; it begins as arrogance — a sense that one has outgrown them. Yahya, given knowledge and wisdom as a child, had every ingredient a young person might use to look down on his elders, and used none of it. Learning made him gentler, not grander.

## Peace on the three loneliest days (ayah 15)

*Wa salāmun ʿalayhi yawma wulida wa yawma yamūtu wa yawma yubʿathu ḥayyā.*

Ibn Kathir frames this ayah as the reward: "after mentioning these beautiful characteristics, Allah mentions his reward for this." And the reward is *salām* — peace, meaning, he says, "that he had security and safety in these three circumstances."

Why these three days in particular? Ibn Kathir quotes Sufyan bin ʿUyaynah — a narration he states "was reported by Ibn Jarir, from Ahmad bin Mansur Al-Marwazi, from Sadaqah bin Al-Fadl, from Sufyan bin ʿUyaynah":

> "The loneliest that a man will ever feel is in three situations. The first situation is on the day that he is born, when he sees himself coming out of what he was in. The second situation is on the day that he dies, when he sees people that he will not see anymore. The third situation is on the day when he is resurrected, when he sees himself in the great gathering."

Read it slowly. Birth: torn out of the only world you have known, into one you did not choose. Death: the faces around you receding, and you going on without them. Resurrection: standing in a crowd beyond counting, and utterly alone in it. Three thresholds no companion can cross with you.

Over exactly these three, Allah lays His own peace. Sufyan bin ʿUyaynah's conclusion is that "Allah has exclusively honored Yahya, the son of Zakariyya, by granting him peace in these situations." Note also the last word of the ayah — *ḥayyan*: the third day is "the day he will be raised up to life (again)". He is raised living, and the security named here reaches him there too.

## What the passage asks of us

These are applications, not tafsir — but each one leans on something said above.

- **Take the Book seriously enough to work at it.** *Bi-quwwah* — as Ibn Kathir has it, learn it well, with zeal and studious effort. The command was given to a child; there is no age at which it does not apply.
- **Do not treat a soft heart as optional, or as luck.** *Ḥanān* is listed among what was given, alongside wisdom. If tenderness is given, it can be asked for.
- **Let purity show up as deeds.** Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj all tie *zakāh* to the righteous deed. Inner cleanness that never becomes action is not what the word means.
- **Measure your religion at home.** Ibn Kathir notes that Yahya's treatment of his parents is attached directly to his obedience to his Lord — and that it covered speech and action, what they commanded and what they forbade.
- **Watch for arrogance before you watch for disobedience.** *Jabbār* comes before *ʿaṣiyy* in the ayah.

The passage began with a boy being handed a Book and ends with peace pronounced over him across birth, death and resurrection. That is the arc: hold fast to what Allah gives you, and He secures you at the moments when nothing else can.

passages.title: Mary withdraws and the angel announces a son
passages.tafsir:
A woman known for her worship steps away from everyone she knows, puts a screen between herself and the world — and finds a stranger standing there. These six ayat are one unbroken scene: the withdrawal (16), the screen and the visitor (17), her terror and her appeal for protection (18), the announcement (19), her astonished question (20), and the answer that ends all discussion — this is easy for Allah, and it is already decreed (21). It is at once a deeply personal moment and, as Ibn Kathir frames it, a demonstration of Allah's power.

## Why this story comes here

Ibn Kathir explains the placement. Allah had just told of Zakariyya, whom He blessed with a righteous, purified and blessed child even in his old age while his wife was barren. Now He tells of Maryam, granted a child named 'Isa with no father involved at all. "Between these two stories there is an appropriate and similar relationship," he writes — which is why, due to their closeness in meaning, Allah mentioned them here together, as well as in Surah Āl-'Imrān and Surah al-Anbiya'. The purpose, Ibn Kathir says, is the same in both: Allah has mentioned these stories to show His servants His ability, the might of His authority, and that He has power over all things. Zakariyya's case stretches what is possible; Maryam's case breaks it open entirely.

## Who Maryam was

Ibn Kathir fills in the background from Āl-'Imrān. She was Maryam bint 'Imran, of the family lineage of Dawud, from a good and wholesome family of the Children of Israel. Her mother had dedicated her freely for the service of Allah — meaning to the service of the Masjid of the Sacred House in Jerusalem. Note the quiet symmetry Ibn Kathir draws out: Zakariyya, Maryam's mother, and Maryam were similar in exactly that aspect, a life handed over to Allah's house.

Allah says of her: **"So her Lord accepted her with goodly acceptance. He made her grow in a good manner"** (3:37). Thus, Ibn Kathir writes, Maryam was raised among the Children of Israel in an honourable way. She was one of the female worshippers, well known for her remarkable acts of worship, devotion and perseverance. She lived under the care of her brother-in-law Zakariyya, a Prophet of the Children of Israel at that time, a great man among them whom they would refer to in their religious matters — and even he saw astonishing miracles occur from her that amazed him: **"Every time Zakariyya entered the Mihrab to visit her, he found her supplied with sustenance. He said: 'O Maryam! From where have you got this?' She said, 'This is from Allah.' Verily, Allah provides to whom He wills, without limit"** (3:37). It has been mentioned, Ibn Kathir adds — and he passes it on in that hedged form — that he would find her with winter fruit during the summer and summer fruit during the winter.

This matters for how you read ayah 16. The woman who withdraws is not a passive figure caught up in events. She is the woman of that ayah in Āl-'Imrān, in whose place of prayer provision arrived from a source she named simply as Allah — long before the angel came.

## Ayah 16: the withdrawal

**"And mention in the Book, Maryam, when she withdrew in seclusion from her family to a place facing east."**

The verb is *intabadhat* (انتبذت). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces it to *nabadh* (نبذ), which means to throw away or to cast away; hence the meaning of *intibādh* is to withdraw from the crowd.

Where exactly did she go? The two commentaries before us describe it differently, and both are worth holding.

- **Ibn Kathir:** this means that she withdrew from them and secluded herself from them. She went to the eastern side of the Sacred Masjid in Jerusalem.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān:** *makānan sharqiyyan* denotes that she retired to a secluded corner of the house facing east. As to *why*, the purpose has been differently explained: some say she had moved there to take a bath, while others say she had moved as usual to a secluded corner on the eastern side of her place of worship in order to offer her prayers. Qurtubi gave preference to the second explanation.

Ibn 'Abbas drew a striking historical conclusion from this word. It is reported from him that he said: "Verily, I am the most knowledgeable of Allah's creation of why the Christians took the east as the direction of devotional worship" — and the reason, he explained, is this very statement of Allah: **"when she withdrew in seclusion from her family to a place facing east."** Therefore, he said, they took the birthplace of 'Isa as their direction of worship. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same from Ibn 'Abbas: this is the reason the Christians face east when offering their prayers, and revere the eastern direction.

## Ayah 17: the screen, and the One sent

**"She placed a screen before them; then We sent to her Our Rūḥ, and he appeared before her in the form of a man in all respects."**

*Fa-ttakhadhat min dūnihim ḥijāban* — Ibn Kathir explains simply: this means that she hid herself from them and concealed herself. Then, Allah sent Jibril to her.

**Who is "Our Rūḥ"?** Mujahid, ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, Wahb bin Munabbih and as-Suddi all commented on this phrase with the same answer: "It means Jibril." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that a majority of scholars hold this view, while some say *Rūḥ* refers to 'Isa himself — that Allah had placed before Maryam the likeness of the son to be born to her. But it judges the former view more appropriate, adding that it is confirmed by the statement that follows: *he took before her the form of a perfect human*.

**Why a human form?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason plainly: it is not given to a human being to see an angel in its real form, because he will be overwhelmed by fright at such an experience. This, it says, is what happened to the Prophet ﷺ in the cave of Hira' on his first encounter with Jibril, and again later on. So Jibril appeared before Maryam in the form of a man — in Ibn Kathir's words, "in the form of a perfect and complete man" — so as not to frighten her.

The commentary sets the next sentence right beside that one, and the two together carry a painful irony. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: he came in the form of a man so as not to frighten her; and when Maryam saw a man near her she became apprehensive of his intentions. Ibn Kathir says the same: when the angel appeared to her in the form of a man, while she was in a place secluded by herself with a partition between her and her people, she was afraid of him and thought that he intended to violate her. The very disguise meant to spare her fear became the occasion of it.

## Ayah 18: her first weapon

**"She said: 'Verily, I seek refuge with the Most Gracious from you, if you do fear Allah.'"**

Read this as what it is: a woman alone, a man where no man should be, and no help within call. What does she reach for first? Not a scream — the Name of Allah.

Ibn Kathir draws out the method: she meant "If you fear Allah" as a means of reminding him of Allah, "and this is what is legislated in defence against evil, so that it may be repulsed with ease. Therefore, the first thing she did was try to make him fear Allah, the Mighty and Sublime." Ibn Jarir reported from 'Asim that Abu Wa'il said, mentioning the story of Maryam: "She knew that the pious person would refrain from committing evil."

Notice too *which* Name she chose. She sought refuge with **ar-Raḥmān** — rendered in these commentaries as the Most Gracious, the Most Beneficent, the All-Merciful. In her most exposed moment, the Name she reached for was the Name of mercy.

**"If you are mindful of Allah"** — *in kunta taqiyyan* — reads oddly at first. Is she making her plea conditional? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two explanations:

1. These are the words which a helpless person would utter to a cruel oppressor, begging him that if he is a believer he should desist from tormenting him. Maryam was entreating the one standing before her in the guise of a man that he should fear Allah and abstain from evil deeds. The expression is therefore **not a precondition for seeking the protection of Allah**, but a condition to make her prayer more effective and inducing.
2. Some other commentators have said the expression is used for emphasis: even if you *are* mindful of Allah I seek His protection; and if the position is otherwise, then I shall seek Allah's refuge with added vehemence. (Mazhari)

Both readings agree on the essential point: her refuge in Allah is unconditional. Only her appeal to *him* is conditioned.

And her words landed. Ibn Kathir mentions — with the wording "it is said," so treat it as a report passed on rather than an established one — that when she mentioned the Name ar-Raḥmān, Jibril fell apart and returned to his true form as an angel. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise says that *some reports have it* that when Jibril heard these words he retreated a little, in reverence of Allah's Name. Both commentaries pass these on with that hedge, and so do we.

## Ayah 19: "I am only a messenger"

**"He said: 'I am only a messenger from your Lord, to give you the gift of a righteous son.'"**

Ibn Kathir: the angel said this to her in response, and in order to remove the fear that she felt within herself — "I am not what you think, but I am the messenger of your Lord." By this he meant, "Allah has sent me to you." That is the whole force of his answer: he is not what she feared, he is an errand. And what he has been sent with is *ghulāman zakiyyan*, a righteous son — the one she feared meant her violation announces instead the gift of a righteous child.

One nuance in the wording. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments on *li-ahaba laki ghulāman* ("that **I** may give you a boy"): here Jibril attributed the gift of the child to himself because Allah had sent him in order that he should breathe into her collar, and this breath would be the means of her conceiving the child — "whereas in reality this gift was by the act of Allah." (Ibn Kathir cites the phrase in the other form, *li-yahaba*, "that **He** may grant you.") The point of the commentary stands either way: the angel is an instrument, never a cause. Means are real; they are not the Doer.

## Ayah 20: her question

**"She said: 'How can I have a son when no man has touched me, nor am I Baghiyy?'"**

Ibn Kathir reads this as amazement, not refusal: Maryam was amazed at this and said, "How can I have a son?" — she said this to mean, "In what way would a son be born to me when I do not have a husband and I do not commit any wicked acts?" She names the only two routes she knows to motherhood and closes both: lawful marriage — *no man has touched me*; unlawful union — *nor am I Baghiyy*.

*Baghiyy* (بغي), Ibn Kathir explains, is a female fornicator. He adds in passing that a hadith has been reported prohibiting the money earned from a *Baghiyy*; the source before us does not name the collection it comes from, so it is left at that.

Her sentence is a self-portrait drawn in two strokes, and it is her honour speaking. Told she will bear a child, her first instinct is to establish, in her own words, that she has no husband and commits no wicked acts.

## Ayah 21: "That is easy for Me"

**"He said: 'Thus says your Lord: That is easy for Me. And We wish to appoint him as a sign to mankind and a mercy from Us, and it is a matter already decreed.'"**

Ibn Kathir: the angel said this to her in response to her question — "Verily, Allah has said that a boy will be born from you even though you do not have a husband and you have not committed any lewdness. Verily, He is Most Able to do whatever He wills." That last sentence is the whole answer. What is impossible by the ordinary means is not thereby difficult for the One who set those means in place.

**"A sign to mankind."** Here Ibn Kathir gives the passage its widest horizon. This means a proof and a sign for mankind of the power of their Maker and Creator, who diversified them in their creation:

- **Adam** — created without a male or a female.
- **Hawwa'** — created from a male, without a female.
- **The rest of their progeny** — from a male and a female.
- **'Isa** — caused to be born from a female without a male.

"Thus, Allah completed the four types of creation of the human being, which proves the perfection of His power and the magnificence of His authority. There is no god worthy of worship except Him and there is no true Lord other than Him." Seen this way, 'Isa is not an exception that breaks the pattern; he is the missing corner that completes it. And notice what the sign *proves* in Ibn Kathir's reading: the power of the Maker and Creator, and that there is no true Lord other than Him. 'Isa himself is, as Ibn Kathir describes him, Allah's servant and Messenger, one of the five Great Messengers.

**"And a mercy from Us."** Ibn Kathir: "We will make this boy a mercy from Allah and a Prophet from among the Prophets. He will call to the worship of Allah and monotheistic belief in Him." He supports it with Āl-'Imrān: **"O Maryam! Verily, Allah gives you the good news of a Word from Him, his name will be al-Masih, 'Isa, the son of Maryam, held in honour in this world and in the Hereafter, and will be one of those who are near to Allah. And he will speak to the people, in the cradle and in manhood, and he will be one of the righteous"** (3:45–46) — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, that he will call to the worship of his Lord in his cradle and as an adult.

**"And it is a matter already decreed."** This is the completion of Jibril's dialogue with Maryam, Ibn Kathir notes: he informed her that this matter was preordained by Allah's power and will. Muhammad bin Ishaq said of it simply: "This means that Allah determined to do this, so there is no avoiding it." Her question had been *how*. The answer ends not with a mechanism but with a decree. Some things are told to us not so that we can work them out, but so that we can submit to them.

## Living it

**Meet danger with the Name of Allah.** Ibn Kathir treats Maryam's response as a model, not merely a report: reminding a wrongdoer of Allah is what is legislated in defence against evil, so that it may be repulsed with ease — and it was the *first* thing she reached for.

**Guard your privacy and your honour as she did.** She withdrew from her family and secluded herself, she hid herself behind a screen, and when a stranger appeared she stated plainly what she was and was not. Ayah 20 is a woman who will not let her chastity be assumed away.

**Ask "how" without doubting "whether."** Maryam asked her question and received an answer; Ibn Kathir reads the question as amazement at what was promised, not resistance to it. That is an honourable way for a believer to stand before something that overturns the ordinary.

**Let "it is easy for Me" resize your problems.** These stories were placed here, Ibn Kathir says, to show Allah's servants His ability, the might of His authority, and that He has power over all things. A barren wife, an old man, a life with no visible way forward — the reply the angel carried is the same in every case: *that is easy for Me*, and *He is Most Able to do whatever He wills*.

passages.title: The birth beneath the palm tree
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** These five ayat take Maryam from the instant of conception to the instant she is ready to face her people. They are held together by a single movement: a woman is driven into total isolation and utter desolation, and there — precisely there — Allah meets her with water, with food, with comfort, and with a plan. Ayah 22 removes her from society; ayah 23 brings her to the lowest point a human heart can reach; ayat 24–26 answer that low point item by item.

## Ayah 22: conception, and the withdrawal

Ibn Kathir explains that when Jibril had spoken to Maryam about what Allah said, **she accepted the decree of Allah**. Many scholars of the predecessors (the Salaf — the earliest generations) mentioned that at that point the angel, who was Jibril, blew into the opening of the garment she was wearing; then the breath descended until it entered into her vagina, and she conceived the child by the leave of Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something easy to miss from the wording a little earlier in the surah, where Jibril says *"to give you a boy"* (19:19). Jibril attributed the gift to himself because Allah had sent him so that he should breathe into her collar, and this breath would be the means of her conceiving the child — **whereas in reality this gift was by the act of Allah.** The angel is the errand, not the source.

Muhammad bin Ishaq recorded what followed. When she had conceived him and filled her water jug at a well, she returned to her people. Her menstrual bleeding then ceased, and she experienced what a pregnant woman experiences — sickness, hunger, change of colour, and even a change in the manner of her speech. After that, no people came to visit any house like they did the house of Zakariyya. The word spread among the Children of Israel, and the people were saying that her partner in fornication must have been Yusuf, because there was no one else in the temple with her except him. **So she hid herself from the people and placed a veil between herself and them.** No one saw her, and she did not see anyone else.

That is the pressure behind the phrase *"and withdrew with him to a remote place."* Her withdrawal is not a whim. She is a woman known for worship whose body is now announcing something her tongue cannot yet explain.

## A note on the miracle itself

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses to insist on the obvious: that Maryam conceived and gave birth to a child **was a miracle**, and miracles, however improbable they may appear, are not beyond Allah's power — rather, the more improbable they are, the more pronounced their miraculous nature.

It then adds a second observation: it cannot be taken as totally impossible either, because according to some books of medical science the fluids found inside the female genitals are not merely a passive agent for conceiving a child; they also have a capacity of being active, and a potential to form a fetus by themselves without an external semen joining them. Maʿārif cites Ibn Sina (Avicenna), the famous medical scientist, who mentioned in his book *Al-Qanun* that in a special disease, which he named *Rajaʼ*, an imperfect form of even the organs of a fetus is shaped in the uterus of a woman without the intermediation of a male semen. So long as this potential is there, it cannot be taken as totally impossible, because some abnormal factor may increase this potential.

## Ayah 23: the trunk of the palm, and the cry

*"Then the pains of labour drove her to the trunk of a palm tree."* Ibn Kathir reads the verb plainly: her pains of labour **compelled** her — forced her — to go to the trunk of a date-palm tree that was at the place where she had secluded herself. She did not choose that spot; pain chose it for her.

**Where was it?** The scholars differed over its location, and Ibn Kathir reports the difference honestly rather than settling it:

- **As-Suddi:** her place of seclusion was to the east, and that was where she would pray at the Sacred House of Jerusalem.
- **Wahb bin Munabbih:** she ran away, and when she reached an area between Ash-Sham and Egypt, she was overcome by labour pains.
- **Wahb, in another narration:** this took place eight miles from the Sacred House of Jerusalem, in a village known as Bayt Al-Lahm (Bethlehem).

Ibn Kathir then adds a note in his own voice: there are Hadiths about the Isra' — the Night Journey of the Prophet ﷺ — reported by **An-Nasa'i** on the authority of Anas, and by **Al-Bayhaqi** on the authority of Shadad bin Aws, that say this took place at Bait Al-Lahm. What he says next, in his own order, is worth reading whole:

> "Allah knows best. This is what is well known that the people all relate from each other. The Christians have no doubt held that the place of this occurrence was Bethlehem and this is what all the people relate. It has been related in a Hadith also, if the Hadith is authentic."

Notice how the "Allah knows best" comes first, and the conditional — *if the Hadith is authentic* — comes last, after he has already registered that this is simply the account people pass along. That caution is itself a lesson in how the classical scholars handled historical detail that faith does not hang upon.

**Her words.** *"Would that I had died before this, and had been forgotten and out of sight!"* Ibn Kathir does not soften this. She knew that she was going to be tested with the birth, that the people would not assist her and would not believe her story, and that after she was known among them as a devout worshipper they now thought she had become a fornicating whore. "Before this," he says, means before *this situation*.

The phrase *nasyan mansiyya* — a forgotten thing, forgotten — is opened by two early authorities:

- **Ibn 'Abbas:** it means, "I wish I had not been created and I was nothing."
- **Qatadah:** it means "something unknown, forgotten, and no one knew who I was."

Ibn Kathir draws a ruling from the ayah: **in it is evidence of the permissibility of wishing for death when a calamity strikes.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān examines that wish more finely, dividing it in two. If her desire for death was due to worldly problems, she may be excused on the ground that she was overpowered by the surrounding circumstances and had reached a state of mind the mystics usually call *ghalabat al-hal* — being overwhelmed by one's condition. But if the desire was due to religious consideration, it was justifiable in its own right: she feared that people would talk ill of her and that she would not be able to endure it with patience, which could be tantamount to committing the sin of showing impatience — and only death could save her from such a predicament. **On that second reading, what she dreads is not the pain but her own failure to bear it patiently.**

## Ayah 24: the voice from below

*"So a voice called to her from below her: Do not grieve — your Lord has placed beneath you a sariy."*

**Two readings, two callers.** Ibn Kathir notes that some reciters read *man tahtaha* — "the one who was below her" called to her — while others read *min tahtiha*, "from below her," with the meaning of a preposition (from) instead of a pronoun (who). The scholars of tafsir then differed over who was calling out:

- **It was Jibril.** Reported from **Ibn 'Abbas** by Al-'Awfi and others, with the reasoning that *'Isa did not speak until she brought him to her people*. Similarly **Sa'id bin Jubayr, Ad-Dahhak, 'Amr bin Maymun, As-Suddi and Qatadah** all said it refers to the angel Jibril — meaning that he called out to her from the bottom of the valley.
- **It was 'Isa himself.** Said by **Mujahid**; likewise Al-Hasan's view, reported by 'Abdur-Razzaq from Ma'mar from Qatadah; and it is one of the two opinions reported from **Sa'id bin Jubayr**, who argued: "Have you not heard Allah saying, *'Then she pointed to him'*?" **Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jarir** preferred this opinion.

Ibn Kathir records both positions from respected early authorities without ruling between them here, noting only that Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jarir preferred the second.

**"Do not grieve."** Notice the order: before the water, before the dates, before the instruction — consolation. Her grief is addressed first.

**What is a *sariy*?** Here too there are two views:

- **A stream of water.** **Al-Bara' bin 'Azib** (reported by Sufyan Ath-Thawri and Shu'bah from Abu Ishaq) said it means a small stream. **Ibn 'Abbas**, in 'Ali bin Abi Talhah's report, said *sariy* means a river; **'Amr bin Maymun** held the same view — "a river for her to drink from"; **Mujahid** said it means river in the Syrian language; **Sa'id bin Jubayr** said a *sariy* is a small flowing river.
- **It refers to 'Isa** — said by **Al-Hasan, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, Muhammad bin 'Abbad bin Ja'far**, one of the two opinions reported from **Qatadah**, and the view of **'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam**.

Ibn Kathir judges that **the first view seems to be the most obvious meaning**, and his reason is the flow of the passage itself: *for this reason*, he says, Allah followed it with the command to shake the palm trunk — "therefore, Allah blessed her by giving her food and drink."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the literal meaning of *sariy* is a small canal, and that Allah caused a small stream to flow at that moment either by His direct command or through Jibril — there are reports supporting both these probabilities.

## Ayah 25: shake the trunk

*"And shake the trunk of this palm tree towards you; it will drop upon you fresh, ripe dates."* Ibn Kathir renders the command: "Grab the trunk of the date-palm tree and shake it towards yourself."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point that has fed generations of believers: **Allah commanded her to shake the date tree, although it was within His power to drop the dates in her lap.** The suggestion here is that one should strive to earn one's living, and that **the struggle for sustenance does not conflict with one's trust in Allah** (this from *Ruh ul-Maʿani*). A woman in the extremity of labour is asked to make an effort — a small, almost token effort against the weight of a palm trunk — and the provision comes down. The effort is real; so is the fact that it was never the effort that produced the dates.

There is also a mercy in *what* she is given. Maʿārif notes that she was directed to eat the dates because **it has been established medically that the use of water and dates gives relief in labour pains**. Ibn Kathir preserves the same insight from an early authority: **'Amr bin Maymun** said, "Nothing is better for the woman confined in childbed than dried dates and fresh dates" — and then he recited this noble ayah.

## Ayah 26: eat, drink, be comforted — and then, silence

*"So eat and drink, and put your heart at ease."* Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase simply: rejoice — **meaning, to be happy.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to an elegance in the sequencing. While describing the means of consolation, water was mentioned first (ayah 24) and then the dates as something to eat (ayah 25); but in the matter of their actual use the order was reversed — eating was enjoined first and then drinking. The reason offered (from *Ruh ul-Maʿani*): normally a person first makes arrangements for drinking water and then for food, especially such food as is more likely to produce thirst; but when it comes to their use the sequence gets reversed — one eats first and then drinks water.

**The vow.** *"And if you see any human being, say: I have vowed a fast to the Most Gracious, so I shall not speak to any human being today."*

What kind of fast? **Anas bin Malik** said: a vow of silence. **Ibn 'Abbas** and **Ad-Dahhak** said the same. Ibn Kathir explains that in their Law, when fasting, it was forbidden for them to eat and to speak — as stated by **As-Suddi, Qatadah and 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd**.

And how does she "say" this if she is not speaking? Ibn Kathir answers the puzzle exactly: **by signalling with gestures, not a statement by speech** — precisely so that she does not negate her oath itself.

'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd fills in the scene, on the view that it was 'Isa who spoke. When 'Isa said, *"Grieve not,"* she said: how can I not grieve when you are with me and I have no husband, nor am I an owned slave woman — what excuse do I have with the people? Woe unto me, if I had only died before this and had been a thing forgotten and unknown. Then 'Isa said to her: *I will suffice you with a statement* — and gave her the words of ayah 26. All of this, Ibn Kathir reports, is from the speech of 'Isa to his mother; **Wahb** said the same as well.

That is the strategy she is handed: she will not argue her own case. Her silence passes the argument to the child, and the child will answer.

**Is such a vow still available to us?** No — and here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic. Before the advent of Islam, silence was also a form of worship, and those who observed this fast were not supposed to speak from dawn to dusk. **Islam cancelled this fast** and made it mandatory to refrain from idle talk, lying and back-biting. Refraining from normal conversation is not a form of worship in Islam any more, and hence to take a vow of silence is also not permissible. Maʿārif cites a hadith reported by **Abu Dawud** from the Prophet ﷺ whose meaning is that a child who has lost his father may not be regarded as an orphan after attaining puberty — the rules pertaining to an orphan cease to apply to him — and that **remaining silent from dawn to dusk is not a form of worship in Islam**. Maʿārif notes that this hadith has been rated *hasan* (sound) by As-Suyuti and Al-ʿAzizi.

So the believer inherits the principle without the practice: the tongue is still to be guarded — but by what it refuses to say, not by refusing to speak.

## Living it

**Consolation comes before instruction.** The voice does not begin by telling Maryam what to do. It begins with *"Do not grieve,"* then gives her water, then food, then a task. When you are helping someone in distress, that order is worth imitating.

**Provision often arrives disguised as the ordinary.** A stream and a palm tree — no thunder, no spectacle. The wonder is in the timing, not the packaging.

**Shake the trunk.** Effort and reliance are not rivals. She was in labour and still asked to pull at a tree; the dates were Allah's, the shaking was hers.

**Not every accusation must be answered by you.** Maryam was given silence, not a speech. There are trials in which the most faithful response is to hold the tongue and let Allah bring the evidence.

**And anguish is not disbelief.** Ibn Kathir reads Maryam's cry in ayah 23 as evidence of the permissibility of wishing for death when a calamity strikes, and Maʿārif reads it charitably — either the overwhelming of the moment, or a righteous fear of failing in patience. The Qur'an preserves the words of a devout worshipper of Allah spoken at her lowest hour, and then, two ayat later, records how completely Allah answered her.

passages.title: Mary accused and the infant Jesus speaks
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat bring the birth narrative to its crisis and its resolution: Maryam walks back into her community carrying her newborn, is met with a public accusation of unchastity, and — held to the command not to speak — says nothing at all. She simply points to the baby, and the baby speaks. What holds the passage together is a single exchange: the people's charge in ayat 27–29, and Allah's answer through the mouth of an infant in ayat 30–33. Maryam does not defend herself. Her defence is placed in a voice her accusers could not argue with.

## She walked in without a defence of her own

Ibn Kathir frames the scene by what came just before it: Allah had commanded Maryam to fast that day and not to speak to any human being, "for verily, her affair would be taken care of and her proof would be established." She accepted the command of Allah, Ibn Kathir says, and readily received His decree — and then took her child and brought him to her people, carrying him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the same moment as an act of confidence: reassured by the signs already given her that Allah would protect her from disgrace, she took the newborn with her and went home.

That is the shape of the whole passage. She was told to hand the case over, and she did.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail about timing: Ibn ʿAsākir narrates through Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that she returned to her people forty days after the birth — that is, after the completion of *nifās*, the bleeding period that follows childbirth. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this via Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī.)

Ibn Kathir also preserves a striking account from Nawf al-Bikālī, reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim. Her people had gone out searching for her — she was from a family blessed with prophethood and nobility — and could find no trace of her. They met a cow herder and described her. He had not seen her, but said that the night before he had seen his cows do something he had never seen them do: prostrating in the direction of a certain valley. ʿAbdullāh bin Ziyād added, from what he had memorised from Sayyār, that the herder also said, "I saw a radiant light." They went towards that valley, and Maryam was coming towards them from that very direction. When she saw them she sat down, holding her child in her lap, and they came and stood over her.

Hold that picture: she seated on the ground with the baby, they standing over her. In this narration the cattle in the field had already turned toward that valley in prostration — while the people arriving from the other direction were about to accuse her of the ugliest thing they could name.

## "A thing *fariyy*" — the weight of the word (ayah 27)

Their opening line is not a question but a verdict: *laqad jiʾti shayʾan fariyyan*.

Ibn Kathir reports that *fariyy* means a mighty thing — this is from Mujāhid, Qatādah, as-Suddī and others; that is, an enormity, something monstrous in scale.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the root: *fary* in Arabic means to cut or to split, and describes work in which a great deal of cutting and chopping is involved. You can hear the physical undertone in the accusation — something torn open, something that rips through the ordinary fabric of things. Abū Ḥayyān noted that the word means anything of preposterous and extraordinary significance, and can be used in a good sense or a bad one; here it is used for something monstrous, and generally the word is applied to what is known to be bad and corrupt in the extreme.

That double edge is worth sitting with. What Maryam had brought genuinely was extraordinary and without precedent, so on Abū Ḥayyān's reading the word itself was not wrong. Only their sense of it was inverted: what they were denouncing as a monstrous disgrace was — as the infant's own first words would shortly establish — a miracle.

## "O sister of Hārūn" (ayah 28)

Then comes the cruellest touch — the appeal to her lineage: *your father was not an indecent man, nor was your mother unchaste*. Ibn Kathir explains their meaning: "You are from a good, pure family, well-known for its righteousness, worship and abstinence from worldly indulgence. How could you do such a thing?"

The address itself, "O sister of Hārūn," has been explained in more than one way, and the sources give the alternatives without forcing a single answer:

- Ibn Kathir's own gloss: "O one resembling Hārūn (Aaron) in worship."
- ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah and as-Suddī: it refers to Hārūn the brother of Mūsā, because she was of his descendants — as the Arabs would say "O brother of Tamīm" to a man of the tribe of Tamīm, or "O brother of Muḍar" to a Muḍarī.
- A third view Ibn Kathir mentions: she was related to a righteous man among them named Hārūn, and she was comparable to him in her abstinence and worship.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the obvious difficulty — Hārūn, the brother and companion of Mūsā (peace be upon them), had died centuries before Maryam's time, so the phrase cannot be literal in that sense — and then records a moment from the Prophet's ﷺ life that bears directly on it. When the Prophet ﷺ sent Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah (may Allah be pleased with him) as his envoy to the people of Najrān, they challenged him with exactly this question: your Qurʼān calls Maryam the sister of Hārūn, yet Hārūn died long before her. Mughīrah did not know the answer. When he returned and reported the exchange, the Prophet ﷺ said: why did you not tell them that it has long been the practice of the believers to name themselves after the prophets, hoping for their *barakah* (blessing), and to claim relationship with them? (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this as reported by Aḥmad, Muslim, Tirmidhī and Nasāʼī.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then reads that statement of the Prophet ﷺ two ways: either the relationship is one of lineage, in the Arab idiom of associating a person with their ancestors; or "Hārūn" here is not Mūsā's brother at all but Maryam's own brother, himself named after the Prophet Hārūn out of reverence — in which case "sister of Hārūn" fits the literal sense of the word.

There is also a hard lesson in the taunt about her parents. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: when someone descended from righteous and pious ancestors commits a sin, the sin is of greater magnitude than the same sin from an ordinary person, because it brings a bad name to the pious elders. So the descendants of righteous people should make extra effort in good deeds and fear Allah at all times.

## The pointing (ayah 29)

*Fa-ashārat ilayh* — "so she pointed to him." Ibn Kathir explains: this was while they were in doubt about her situation, condemning her circumstances, saying whatever they wished to say, slandering her and falsely accusing her of a horrendous act. That day she was fasting and keeping silent. So she referred all speech to the child and directed them to his address to them.

Maymūn bin Mahrān explains her gesture: "She indicated, 'Speak to him.'" And they said: after she has come to us with this calamity, she now commands us to speak to one who is a child in the cradle! As-Suddī reports their fury even more sharply: "Her mocking us, to the extent of commanding us to speak to this child, is worse to us than her fornication."

Notice what her silence costs her. In the moment of pointing, she is not merely accused of immorality; she is now also accused of mockery — of playing games with her accusers. Ibn Kathir says plainly that they scoffed because they thought she was mocking them and playing with them. She absorbs a second insult on top of the first, and still does not open her mouth. The command she had been given was to be silent, and she keeps it right to the edge.

## "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah" (ayah 30)

Then the infant speaks — and Ibn Kathir draws attention to the order of his words, because the order is the point.

"The first thing that he said was a declaration of the lofty honour of his Lord and His being free of having a child. Also, he affirmed that he himself was a worshipper of his Lord."

Before he says a word about his mother's innocence, before he says anything about prophethood, he says *ʿabdullāh* — I am Allah's servant. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the reason explicit: in his very first words ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) made clear that although his birth was a miracle, he himself was not divine but only a servant of Allah — and this was to eliminate forever the possibility that people would take him as an object of worship on account of that miraculous birth. His first sentence closes the door that his miraculous birth might otherwise have left open.

Both commentaries preserve the physical scene. Nawf al-Bikālī says that when they said what they said to his mother, ʿĪsā was nursing at her breast; at their statement he released the breast from his mouth and reclined on his left, saying: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah; He has given me the Scripture and made me a Prophet" — and he kept speaking until he reached "as long as I live." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that he moved over onto his left side facing them and raised his index finger as he spoke.

"He has given me the Scripture and made me a Prophet," says Ibn Kathir, "was a declaration of innocence for his mother from the immorality that was attributed to her." The argument needs no elaboration, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it directly: his being a Prophet was proof enough that his birth was free from any blemish. By announcing his prophethood he dispelled the people's doubts and cleared his mother of the charge.

Why the past tense, "He *has* given me the Scripture," when the Book and the mission were still decades away? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: no prophet has been granted prophethood and a sacred book before the age of forty, so the infant is conveying in advance that he would be given both at the proper time; the past tense is used because the matter is certain to occur. It cites as a parallel the Prophet's ﷺ statement that he was bestowed prophethood even before Ādam (peace be upon him) was yet in the process of his creation — a promise so firm and final that it is spoken of as already done.

## "Blessed wherever I am" (ayah 31)

What is this blessedness — *mubārak*, "made blessed"? Ibn Kathir gathers the early answers. Mujāhid, ʿAmr bin Qays and ath-Thawrī all said it means: "He made me a teacher of goodness." In another narration from Mujāhid: "a person of great benefit."

Ibn Jarīr reports from Wuhayb bin al-Ward, a freed slave of the Banī Makhzūm, that a scholar once met a scholar with more knowledge than himself and asked, "May Allah have mercy upon you — what acts of mine should I perform openly?" The other replied: "Commanding good and forbidding evil, for verily, it is the religion of Allah, which He sent His Prophets with to His servants." Then it was asked what ʿĪsā's blessing consisted of, and Wuhayb replied: "Commanding good and forbidding evil wherever he was."
