So *mubārak* here is not a decorative aura around a holy man. On these readings it is portable usefulness — being the kind of servant in whom Allah puts benefit for others in every place he is set down. That is a blessing anyone can pray for.

## "Ṣalāh and Zakāh as long as I live"

The verb is *awṣānī*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it comes from *waṣiyyah*, which normally means to bequeath, but when used in the context of issuing an order it carries emphatic force — hence "enjoined." Allah did not merely tell him to pray and to give; He charged him with both, and with observing them diligently. *Ṣalāh* here is the prescribed prayer; *zakāh* is the obligatory charity due on wealth.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that prayer and obligatory charity have been made obligatory in the sacred law of every prophet from Ādam to the last of the Prophets, Muhammad ﷺ, though their details vary from code to code, and that both were obligatory in the law of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) too. It also raises a fair objection: ʿĪsā was never wealthy — he never built himself a house nor accumulated material riches — so why enjoin zakāh on him? The answer given is that the injunction is general in form: whoever possesses a certain level of wealth (*niṣāb*, the threshold at which zakāh becomes due) is liable. Whenever his wealth reached that threshold he was required to pay; if it stayed below it throughout his life, no liability ever arose. There is no conflict with the general rules governing zakāh.

"As long as I live" means the injunction is forever — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the reference is to life in this world, since these duties can only be performed here. Ibn Kathir sets the phrase beside Allah's word to Muhammad ﷺ: "And worship your Lord until there comes unto you the certainty" — that is, death (15:99). There is no retirement from worship in any prophet's law.

Ibn Kathir then records a point of ʿaqīdah (creed — what a Muslim holds as belief) from Mālik bin Anas, reported by ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin al-Qāsim. Commenting on this very phrase, Mālik said: "Allah informed him of what would be of his affair until his death. This is the firmest evidence against the people who deny Allah's preordained decree." An infant is informed of, and announces, what his lifelong practice will be — which on Mālik's reading could not be stated unless it were already known and decreed by Allah.

## "And dutiful to my mother" (ayah 32)

Ibn Kathir: this means Allah has commanded him to treat his mother well. And he observes the placement — ʿĪsā mentions it directly after mentioning obedience to his Lord, because Allah often combines the command to worship Him with obedience to parents, as in "And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him and that you be dutiful to your parents" (17:23) and "Give thanks to Me and to your parents. Unto Me is the final destination" (31:14).

There is something else here that the wording quietly proves. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points it out: only the mother is mentioned, not both parents — from which it is implied that his birth was a miracle, without a father. And such a discourse coming from an infant was itself a miracle proving that miraculous birth.

Think about what this line does for Maryam personally. She has been publicly shamed for what she carried; the first public speech of the one she carried declares that Allah made him good to her.

Then: "and He has made me not arrogant, unblessed" (*jabbāran shaqiyyan*). Ibn Kathir explains: Allah has not made him too proud or arrogant to worship Him, to obey Him, and to be dutiful to his mother, and thus unblessed. Note the pairing the two words imply: on Ibn Kathir's reading, arrogance and wretchedness travel together, and what stands against both is worship of Allah and kindness to a parent.

## "Peace be upon me" on the three hardest days (ayah 33)

The speech closes with peace named over three moments: the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.

Ibn Kathir reads this as the seal on everything ʿĪsā has just said about himself: it is his affirmation that he is a worshipper of Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, and a creature created by Allah — that he will live, die and be resurrected, just like the other creatures Allah has created. However, in these situations, which are the most difficult situations for Allah's creatures, he will have peace. May Allah's peace and blessings be upon him.

So the passage ends where it began. The people asked how a child in a cradle could speak; the child's answer was, from first word to last, that he is a servant — born, dying, and raised, exactly as created servants are. His mother's vindication and his own creaturehood are delivered in the same breath.

## What to carry away

**When you are wronged and you know Allah knows.** Maryam was given a command that felt like the opposite of self-defence, and she kept it while the insults doubled. Allah's promise — that her affair would be taken care of and her proof established — was fulfilled in a way no argument of hers could have achieved.

**Guard the name you inherited.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's note on "your father was not an indecent man" cuts both ways: the children of righteous people carry a heavier account, and should work harder and fear Allah more, precisely because their failures wound more than themselves.

**Ask to be *mubārak* wherever you are.** On the reading of Mujāhid, ath-Thawrī and Wuhayb bin al-Ward, that means being a teacher of good, a person of great benefit, someone who commands good and forbids evil in whatever place Allah sets him down — not in one favoured setting, but *ayna mā kuntu*, "wherever I am."

**Prayer, charity, and your mother, for life.** The infant's own summary of his religion is remarkably plain: I am Allah's servant; He enjoined on me ṣalāh and zakāh as long as I live; and He made me dutiful to my mother. There is no age at which any of the three is finished.

passages.title: Allah takes no son; the sects divide
passages.tafsir:
Ibn Kathir opens this passage with Allah addressing His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ: *This is the story which We have related to you about 'Isa*, upon him be peace. Over these four ayat Allah names him, states what does not befit His own majesty, quotes 'Isa's own words about who his Lord is, and then reports what people went on to do with that clarity. One question runs through the whole unit — who is 'Isa? — answered by Allah in ayat 34–35, answered by 'Isa himself in ayah 36, and left standing against the disagreement of the sects in ayah 37.

## "That is 'Isa, son of Maryam" — the correct position between two extremes

The demonstrative "that" points back over the story Allah has just related and puts a seal on it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene sharply. The beliefs of the Jews and the Christians about 'Isa stood at opposite extremes: the Christians raised him to such a level of reverence that they regarded him as the son of Allah, while the Jews denigrated him maliciously, calling him — Allah forbid — the illegitimate son of Yusuf the carpenter. Allah has pointed out the error in both of these views in these ayat and clarified the correct position. And notice how the passage does it: simply by naming him accurately, *'Isa, son of Maryam*. Not less than that, and not more.

## A word of truth: how the phrase is recited

The phrase *qawl al-ḥaqq* in ayah 34 is one of the places where the transmitted recitations of the Qur'an differ, and the sense shifts with them.

**With ḍammah — *qawlu'l-ḥaqq*.** Ibn Kathir reports this as the recitation of most of the reciters, with the phrase standing as the subject and referring to 'Isa himself: he *is* the word of truth. Ibn Kathir considers this the most apparent meaning grammatically, and finds support for it in Allah's words after the story of 'Isa elsewhere: *(This is) the truth from your Lord, so be not of those who doubt* (3:60).

**With fathah — *qawla'l-ḥaqq*.** Ibn Kathir names 'Asim and 'Abdullah bin 'Amir as reciting it this way, referring to the story in its entirety, the story people differed about. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, treating this as the normal reading, explains it as an implied *aqūlu qawla'l-ḥaqq* — "I say the word of truth."

**A third report.** It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited it *qāla'l-ḥaqqa*, which means that 'Isa spoke the truth.

On the first of these, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Qurtubi: calling 'Isa "a word of truth" is analogous to the title given to him, *kalimatu'Llāh*, the Word of Allah — a title that denotes that he was born directly by the word of Allah, having no connection with an apparent cause in this world. It is worth noticing what that title is saying: it speaks of *how he came into being*. And the testimony the Prophet ﷺ taught, which we will come to at the end, joins that very title to the words "Allah's servant and Messenger" in a single sentence.

And what of *"about which they doubt"* (*yamtarūn*)? Ibn Kathir explains that this means the people of falsehood and the people of truth are in disagreement — those who believe in him and those who disbelieve. Truth is being stated here in full awareness that people are arguing about it.

## Ayah 35: what does not befit Allah

*It is not for Allah to take a son.* Ibn Kathir renders it: it does not befit the majesty of Allah that He should beget a son. Sit with the wording for a moment — the denial is framed in terms of what *befits* His majesty. Then comes *subḥānahu* — Glory be to Him — which Ibn Kathir explains as: glory be unto Him, He is far exalted above that which these ignorant, wrongdoing, transgressing people say about Him. Ibn Kathir also notes where this praise falls: when Allah mentioned that He created 'Isa as a servant and a Prophet, He then extolled Himself.

Then the passage grounds the denial in something positive: *When He decrees a thing, He only says to it: "Be!" — and it is.* Whenever He wants something, says Ibn Kathir, He merely commands it and it happens as He wills. And Ibn Kathir brings the decisive parallel: *Verily, the likeness of 'Isa before Allah is the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him: "Be" — and he was. (This is) the truth from your Lord, so be not of those who doubt* (3:59–60). Adam came into existence with no father at all, from dust, by that same command. A creating that works by *kun* needs no lineage.

## Ayah 36: 'Isa's own words

*Surely Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.*

Ibn Kathir tells us that this was among the things 'Isa said to his people while he was in his cradle: that Allah was his Lord and their Lord, and he commanded them to worship Him alone. This is the passage's quiet argument. The correction of the two extremes is not imposed on 'Isa from the outside centuries later; it is his own word, spoken while he was still in the cradle. And note where he places himself in that sentence — *my Lord and your Lord* — on the same side of the line as his listeners: a servant among servants of the One they are all being told to worship.

*This is a straight path.* Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: "That which I have come to you with from Allah is the straight path" — meaning the path is correct; whoever follows it will be rightly guided, and whoever opposes it will deviate and go astray. Notice how concrete the definition of the straight path is here. It is not a mood or a sentiment. Its content is *fa'budūhu* — so worship Him, Him alone.

## Ayah 37: then the sects differed

*Then the sects differed among themselves.* Ibn Kathir explains that the opinions of the People of the Book differed concerning 'Isa **even after the explanation of his affair and the clarification of his situation**. That phrase carries the weight of the ayah: the splintering did not happen because the evidence was thin. It happened after clarity. They disagreed about his being the servant of Allah, His Messenger, His Word that He cast upon Maryam, and a spirit from Him. Ibn Kathir lays out the positions:

- One group — whom he identifies as the majority of the Jews — determined that he was a child of fornication, and that his speaking in his cradle was merely sorcery.
- Another group said that it was Allah Who was speaking, not 'Isa.
- Others said that he was the son of Allah.
- Some said that he was the third part of a divine trinity with Allah.
- Yet others said that he was the servant of Allah and His Messenger. **This last view is the statement of truth, which Allah guided the believers to.**

Ibn Kathir notes that a report carrying this meaning has come from 'Amr bin Maymun, Ibn Jurayj, Qatadah and others among the Salaf (the early generations) and the Khalaf (those who came after them).

Read that list against ayah 36 and something clarifies. The saved position is not a compromise negotiated between two extremes. It is simply what 'Isa said about himself from the cradle: Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. The four errors are four different ways of not listening to him — one by slandering him, one by taking the speech in the cradle away from him, two by raising him past what he claimed.

## "Woe to the disbelievers from the meeting of a great Day"

Ibn Kathir calls this a threat and a severe warning for those who lie about Allah, invent falsehood, and claim that He has a son. The "great Day" here, he says, refers to the Day of Resurrection.

But then he addresses the question a reader is bound to ask: if the offence is this grave, why does nothing happen? His answer is that Allah has given them respite until the Day of Resurrection, and has delayed their term out of gentleness and confident reliance upon His divine decree overcoming them; Allah does not hasten the affair of those who disobey Him. He supports this with a hadith collected in the Two Sahihs:

> "Verily, Allah gives respite to the wrongdoer until He seizes him and he will not be able to escape Him."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then recited: *Such is the punishment of your Lord when He punishes the towns while they are doing wrong. Verily, His punishment is painful, (and) severe* (11:102).

And in the Two Sahihs it is also reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "No one is more patient with something harmful that he hears than Allah. Verily, they attribute to Him a son, while He is the One Who provides them sustenance and good health."

Sit with that for a moment. The hadith sets two things side by side in one breath: the slander, and the sustenance. The very health that lets a man say such a thing about his Maker is a gift from that Maker, given while the words are still in his mouth. Ibn Kathir then closes off any misreading of the delay with two further ayat: *And many a township did I give respite while it was given to wrongdoing. Then I punished it. And to Me is the (final) return* (22:48), and *Consider not that Allah is unaware of that which the wrongdoers do, but He gives them respite up to a Day when the eyes will stare in horror* (14:42). Respite is not approval, and delay is not inattention.

## The testimony that saves

Against the false positions of ayah 37, Ibn Kathir sets an authentic hadith that is agreed upon (in Al-Bukhari and Muslim), on the authority of 'Ubadah bin As-Samit, who said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Whoever testifies that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah alone, Who has no partners, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and that 'Isa was Allah's servant and Messenger, and His Word that He cast upon Maryam, and a spirit from Him, and that Paradise and Hell are both real, then Allah will admit him into Paradise regardless of whatever he did."

Look at how carefully that testimony is balanced. 'Isa is *servant and Messenger* — which is exactly the position Ibn Kathir identified as the statement of truth, and which refuses every exaltation beyond his rank. And he is *His Word cast upon Maryam, and a spirit from Him* — which refuses every slander against his origin. Hold both halves and you are standing exactly where ayah 36 left you. Drop either half and you have landed among the differing sects of ayah 37.

## Living it

**Say *subḥānahu* and mean it.** The passage teaches the reflex of glorifying Allah the moment something unworthy is attributed to Him — not as a slogan, but as a recognition that He is far exalted above what such people say about Him.

**Honour 'Isa properly.** Ibn Kathir's list puts slander and deification alike outside the statement of truth. A believer defends 'Isa's honour as firmly as he refuses to raise him past his rank; both are what the truth requires, and neither is a concession to anyone.

**Do not read delay as permission.** When falsehood about Allah goes unanswered and wrongdoers seem untouched, the hadith of the Two Sahihs tells you what you are actually watching: respite, from a Lord who does not hasten the affair of those who disobey Him, and who is not unaware of what the wrongdoers do.

**Keep the definition of the path simple.** *So worship Him — this is a straight path.* Whoever follows it will be rightly guided; whoever opposes it will deviate and go astray. Everything else in the passage is defending that one sentence.

passages.title: The Day of Regret when all is decided
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** The commentary of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathered here looks back to the verses just before ours, where Allah settles the truth about ʿĪsā the son of Maryam against two opposite extremes: the Christians exalting him to the point of regarding him as the son of Allah, and the Jews denigrating him maliciously. From that dispute the sūrah turns to its ending — the Day when everyone who argued, denied and drifted comes before Allah. The three ayat move as one. Ayah 38 shows those people at the Resurrection with their hearing and sight suddenly, uselessly perfect. Ayah 39 commands that they be warned of that Day *now*, while warning can still do something. Ayah 40 closes the case by naming who actually owns the world they are so absorbed in. Holding all three together is a contrast between two "todays": the today they are asleep in, and the Day they will see everything in.

## Ayah 38 — senses that arrive too late

**"How clearly will they see and hear, the Day when they will appear before Us! But the wrongdoers today are in plain error."**

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is "informing about the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection that they will be made to have the clearest hearing and sight." The phrase, he says, "means that no one will hear and see better than they will." The very faculties they refused to use are handed back to them at full strength, at the one moment they can no longer be spent.

Ibn Kathir places beside it Allah's words elsewhere: *"And if you only could see when the criminals hang their heads before their Lord (saying): 'Our Lord! We have now seen and heard.'"* (32:12). That is exactly the tone — the admission is finally honest, and finally worthless. Ibn Kathir comments that they will say it "when it will not benefit them, nor will it be of any use to them. If they had used these senses properly before seeing the torment, then it would have brought them some benefit and saved them from the Allah's punishment."

Then the ayah turns on a single word — *lākin*, "but." Ibn Kathir glosses "today" as "now, in the life of this world," and "in plain error" with a devastating summary: "They do not hear, see or think. When they are requested to follow guidance, they are not guided and they succumb to those things that do not benefit them."

Notice what that does. The same people are described twice in one ayah, in two different times. On the Day they appear before Allah: perfect ears, perfect eyes. Today, with the Qurʼān being recited to them and the signs standing all around them: they do not hear, see or think. The organs were never the problem. Sight and hearing are not really about eyes and ears at all — they are about what a person is willing to let in. And the tragedy is the sequencing: the clarity comes, in full, one moment after it could have saved them.

**"The day when they will appear before Us."** Ibn Kathir identifies it plainly: the Day of Resurrection. Both renderings before us — "the Day they will come" and "the day when they will appear before Us" — describe an arrival. Everyone in this passage is already travelling. The arrival is not in question; only the state one arrives in is.

## Ayah 39 — the Day of Ḥasrah

**"And warn them of the Day of grief and regrets, when the case has been decided, while (now) they are in a state of carelessness, and they believe not."**

*Ḥasrah* is a word English cannot hold in one hand, and our sources reach for it from four different sides: "the Day of grief and regrets," "the Day of Distress," "the Day of Remorse," "the Day of Regret." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this is the Day of Judgment, and that it is called the Day of Remorse "because on that day persons consigned to Hell as punishment for their evil deeds will regret their disregard of the righteous way of life, and wish that if they had lived the life of true believers, they too would have been in Paradise instead of being punished in Hell." That is the ache the word is carrying: not pain alone, but the realisation that something was within reach and was let go.

Ibn Kathir keeps the command broad: *warn the creation* of the Day of Distress. The warning is not aimed only at the openly hostile; it is for everyone, because the disease named next — heedlessness — is not a disease of enemies alone.

**"When the case has been decided."** Ibn Kathir explains this as the moment "when the people of Paradise and the people of Hell will be sorted out, and everyone will reach his final abode which he was destined to remain in forever." That is what makes the regret unbearable: not the pain by itself, but the fact that the file is now closed. In this world every regret has an unspoken clause attached — *but I can still fix it.* On that Day the clause is gone.

**"While (now) they are in a state of carelessness."** Ibn Kathir again anchors it in the present: "today, in the present life of this world" — "with the warning of the Day of grief and regret, they are heedless." And *"they believe not"* means, in his words, "they do not believe that it is true." That is the double lock. Not merely unaware, but unpersuaded that there is anything to be aware of.

## From the Sunnah: the ram that is slaughtered

Ibn Kathir reports that Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Saʿid said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> (When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Hellfire enter the Hellfire, death will be brought in the form of a handsome ram and it will be placed between Paradise and the Hellfire. Then, it will be said, "O people of Paradise, do you know what this is?" Then, they will turn their gazes and look, and they will say, "Yes, this is death." Then, it will be said, "O people of the Hellfire, do you know what this is?" Then, they will turn their gazes and look, and they will say, "Yes, this is death." Then, the order will be given for it to be slaughtered and it will be said, "O people of Paradise, eternity and no more death, O people of Hellfire, eternity and no more death.")

Then — and this is the point for our ayah — the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited *"And warn them of the Day of grief and regret, when the case has been decided, while (now) they are in a state of carelessness, and they believe not,"* and then, in Ibn Kathir's words, "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made a gesture with his hand and said, **(The people of this life are in the state of heedlessness of this life.)**" Ibn Kathir adds: "Thus recorded Imam Ahmad and it was also recorded by Al-Bukhari and Muslim in their Sahihs with wording similar to this."

Sit with the scene the Prophet ﷺ tied to this ayah. Death — the one certainty every human being organises their denial around — is itself brought out and slaughtered. Both parties recognise it; both have their answer confirmed forever. And then the Prophet ﷺ turns from that immense scene to the state of the people living right now. The ayah is not describing a distant tribe. It is describing the ordinary condition of anyone who has not deliberately woken himself up.

## Two houses, and the regret of the saved

Ibn Kathir also reports from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud, in a story he mentioned, that "there is not a soul except that it will see a residence in Paradise and a residence in the Hellfire, and this will be the Day of distress." The people of the Hellfire will see the residence Allah had prepared for them if they had believed, and it will be said to them: "If you had believed and worked righteous deeds, you would have had this, which you see in Paradise" — and they will be overcome with distress and grief. Likewise the people of Paradise will see the residence that is in the Hellfire, and it will be said to them: "If Allah had not bestowed His favor upon you" (that is, this would have been your place).

So the regret is not only over what was done; it is over what was *available*. Two doors were standing open for every single soul, and each soul will be shown the one it did not walk through. For the people of the Hellfire that sight is the distress itself. For the people of Paradise the same sight is pure gratitude — and note carefully what they are told: not "you earned your escape," but "if Allah had not bestowed His favor upon you." Salvation is named as a gift, not a wage.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that "even those who have been rewarded with Paradise will feel a different kind of remorse," and cites two reports. Al-Ṭabarānī and Abū Yaʿlā have quoted this saying of the Prophet ﷺ on the authority of Sayyidnā Muʿādh (may Allah be pleased with him): **"The people of Paradise will regret only one thing, namely those moments which were spent without the remembrance of Allah."** And Al-Baghawī narrated, quoting Abū Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Everyone will experience remorse and regret after death." When the Companions asked what that remorse and regret would be about, he ﷺ explained that those who acted righteously will regret not having performed more righteous deeds, which would have helped them attain a higher position in Paradise, while the evildoers will repent their evil actions and sins (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazharī).

That is a searching thought. Even in a place where nothing can hurt you, one thing still stings: an empty minute. Not a sinful minute — an *empty* one. If the successful will one day wish they had filled more of their time with the remembrance of Allah, then the cheapest possible insurance against the Day of Regret is the remembrance you can begin in the next ten seconds, with no equipment and no delay.

## Ayah 40 — who is left when everyone is gone

**"Verily, We will inherit the earth and whatsoever is thereon. And to Us they all shall be returned."**

Ibn Kathir unfolds it: Allah "is informing that He is the Creator, the Owner and the Controller of all matters. All of the creation will be destroyed and only He, the Most High and Most Holy, will remain. There is no one who can claim absolute ownership and control of affairs besides Him. He is the Inheritor of all His creation. He is the Eternal, Who will remain after they are gone and He is the Judge of their affairs."

An inheritor, in Ibn Kathir's description, is the One who remains after the others are gone. That is what makes the ayah quietly staggering: everything people spend their heedlessness on — the earth, and "whatsoever is thereon," the owners themselves — comes back to Allah, who alone remains.

And Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion that turns this from cosmology into comfort. Because Allah is the Owner, the Eternal and the Judge, "therefore, no soul will be done any injustice, nor wronged even the weight of a mosquito or an atom." The One who inherits it all will not shortchange anybody. The ayah that sounds like a threat to the heedless is, for the wronged believer, the strongest possible guarantee.

The closing phrase — *"and to Us they all shall be returned"* — links back to ayah 38's "the day when they will appear before Us." The passage begins with their arrival and ends with their return; the Day of Regret sits in the middle.

Ibn Kathir records that Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Hazm bin Abi Hazm Al-Qutaʿi that ʿUmar bin ʿAbdul-ʿAziz wrote to ʿAbdul-Hamid bin ʿAbdur-Rahman, who was the governor of Kufah: "Verily, Allah prescribed death for His creatures when He created them and He determined their final destination. He said in that which He revealed in His truthful Book, which He guarded with His knowledge and made His angels testify to its preservation, that He will inherit the earth and all who are on it, and they will all be returned to Him." Of everything a letter to a governor might open with, this is what he put at the top: death is prescribed, the destination is fixed, and the earth and everyone on it return to Allah.

## Living it

**The warning is the mercy.** Ayah 39 does not say "regret is coming, brace yourself." It says *warn them* — which means the Day of Regret is still, at this moment, avoidable. Every ayah of warning you read is proof that your file is still open, that the case has not yet been decided.

**Use the senses now.** Ibn Kathir's point in ayah 38 is that hearing and sight only ever helped anyone *before* the torment came into view. Faith is not finally about information — those people will have the clearest possible hearing and sight, and it will not save them. It is about responding while responding still counts. When the Qurʼān is recited to you and it lands as background noise, that is precisely the condition ayah 38 is diagnosing.

**Heedlessness is the normal state, not the exception.** The Prophet ﷺ made a gesture with his hand and said, "The people of this life are in the state of heedlessness of this life." Nobody drifts *into* attentiveness. Remembering Allah, reading, letting the warning actually land — these are the deliberate acts by which a person keeps stepping out of the default.

**Aim above the pass mark.** Since even the people of Paradise will wish they had done more, the sane response is not to calculate the minimum, but to fill the empty minutes — the queue, the commute, the walk — with the remembrance of Allah, so that there is less to wish back on a Day when nothing can be wished back.

passages.title: Abraham pleads with his idolatrous father
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Allah commands His Prophet ﷺ to recite the story of Ibrahim (Abraham), and what follows is a single unbroken speech: four short appeals a son makes to an idol-worshipping father, each one opening with the same tender word — *yā abati*, "O my dear father." What holds ayat 41–45 together is not only the subject but the voice. It is one continuous plea, built in four moves, and it teaches as much about *how* to call someone to the truth as about *what* to say.

## Why this story, and why to these listeners

Ibn Kathir reads the command of ayah 41 — "And mention in the Book, Ibrahim" — as Allah instructing Muhammad ﷺ: "Recite this to your people who are worshipping idols and mention to them what happened with Ibrahim, the intimate Friend (*Khalil*) of the Most Beneficent."

The force of that is easy to miss. Those idol-worshipping Arabs were, as Ibn Kathir notes, Ibrahim's own descendants, and they claimed to follow his religion. So this is not a distant biography being read out to strangers; it is being read to people who traded on Ibrahim's name. And notice exactly what they are to be told about him: Ibn Kathir says they are to be informed that he was a truthful Prophet, and told "about what took place with his father and how he forbade him from worshipping idols." The one thing they are made to hear about the forefather they claim is that he stood against idol worship — inside his own family.

## "A man of truth, a Prophet" (ayah 41)

Before a single word of the conversation, Allah certifies the speaker: *ṣiddīqan nabiyyā* — "a man of truth, a Prophet."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *ṣiddīq* is a Qur'anic term scholars have defined in more than one way. Some say it is applied to one who has never told a lie in his life. Others describe *ṣiddīq* as one who is truthful in his beliefs, his words and his deeds together — his utterances truly reflect his beliefs, and his actions in turn match his beliefs and words. Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī and Mazharī adopt this second meaning.

That second definition is the one that makes ayah 41 a doorway into ayat 42–45. A man whose conduct matches his convictions is exactly the man who will say aloud, in front of an idol and in front of his own father, what he actually believes. The certification is not decoration; it introduces the speech that follows.

Maʿārif adds two careful qualifications. First, *ṣiddīqiyyah* (truthfulness) has degrees — those who fall within the definition are placed at different levels. Second, on the relation between the two titles in the ayah: only a prophet can be a true *ṣiddīq*, and while every prophet is gifted with this quality, not everyone who has it is a prophet. A believer who follows in the footsteps of his prophet and attains this exalted station can also be called *ṣiddīq*. The Qur'an itself confers the title *ṣiddīqah* on Sayyidah Maryam, despite the view of the overwhelming majority that she was not a prophet, and that a woman cannot be a prophet.

## Four times he says "O my dear father"

Here is the heart of the passage, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats it as a lesson in how to give counsel to elders.

The word *yā abati* in Arabic conveys deep respect and intense love for one's father. Ibrahim places it at the head of *every one* of the four sentences — ayat 42, 43, 44, and 45. He is holding two things at once that most people cannot hold together. On one side, as Maʿārif describes it: he finds his father living a life of unbelief and polytheism, and calling other people to follow him in a life of sin — the very things Ibrahim was sent to eradicate. On the other side, there is the filial love and respect he feels towards his father. Maʿārif calls his address "a perfect example of moderation and restraint," and asks us to note how well he combines the two conflicting feelings.

Look at what is *absent*. Maʿārif points out that there is not a single derogatory word in the address that could hurt his father's feelings — words such as *infidel* or *sinner* have been carefully avoided.

And look at the sequence Maʿārif traces through the four sentences:

1. **Ayah 42** — guided by prophetic wisdom, he merely invites his father's attention to the helplessness and insensitivity of his idols, so that his father might himself realise the fallacy of his beliefs.
2. **Ayah 43** — he mentions the prophetic knowledge that was granted to him by Allah.
3. **Ayat 44 and 45** — in the third and fourth sentences he warns his father against the Divine wrath that infidelity and idolatry invite.

Notice the direction of travel: he begins with a question his father could answer for himself, and only afterwards comes to the warning. He does not open with the punishment.

## The question that answers itself (ayah 42)

"O my dear father! Why do you worship that which hears not, sees not and cannot avail you in anything?"

He does not tell his father he is wrong; he asks him *why*. And the description carries the argument: a thing that does not hear, does not see, and — as Ibn Kathir glosses it — "will not benefit you, nor can they protect you from any harm."

That is the whole method Maʿārif describes: no insult, no verdict, just his father's attention drawn to the helplessness and insensitivity of the idols, so that the man might see the fallacy himself.

## Knowledge that outranks age (ayah 43)

"O my dear father! Verily, there has come to me the knowledge of that which came not unto you. So follow me, I will guide you to the straight path."

This is the most delicate sentence in the passage, because a son is asking a father to follow *him*. Ibn Kathir catches exactly what Ibrahim is negotiating: "Even though I am from your loins and you see me as inferior to you because I am your son, know that I have received knowledge from Allah that you do not know and it has not reached you."

Note how the claim is framed. He does not say *I am cleverer than you*; he says knowledge has *come to* him — received from Allah, as Maʿārif also puts it, prophetic knowledge that was granted to him by Allah. The authority he invokes is not his own standing. And the invitation that follows — "follow me, I will guide you to the straight path" — Ibn Kathir explains as "a straight path that will carry you to the desired objective and save you from that which is dreaded (Hell)." Ibrahim is not asking his father to lose an argument. He is offering him a rescue, and offering to walk it with him.

## The one actually being obeyed (ayah 44)

"O my dear father! Worship not Shaytan. Verily, Shaytan has been a rebel against the Most Gracious."

This is the turn that reframes everything. His father would have said he worshipped idols, not Shaytan. But Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: "Do not obey him by worshipping these idols. He invites to this (idolatry) and he is pleased with it." Obedience *is* the worship here. The one who invites to a thing and is pleased with it is the one being served by it.

Ibn Kathir supports this reading with two other ayat. Allah says, "Did I not command you, O Children of Adam, that you should not worship Shaytan. Verily, he is a plain enemy to you" (36:60). And: "They invoke nothing but females [idols] besides Him (Allah), and they invoke nothing but Shaytan, a persistent rebel!" (4:117) — a single act of invocation, described both as calling on idols and as calling on Shaytan.

Then the reason: *inna ash-shayṭāna kāna lir-raḥmāni ʿaṣiyyā*. Ibn Kathir explains this as meaning Shaytan was "obstinate and too arrogant to obey his Lord. Therefore, Allah expelled him and made him an outcast." And he draws the conclusion Ibrahim intends: "do not follow him or you will become like him."

That is the logic of ayah 44 in full. Shaytan's rebellion did not merely make him guilty; it got him cast out. To follow a road is to arrive where it leads. Notice, too, the name of Allah under which Ibrahim frames the rebellion: *ar-Raḥmān*, the Most Gracious — and it is that same name he will use again in the very next sentence.

## "I fear for you" (ayah 45)

"O my dear father! Verily, I fear lest a torment from the Most Gracious should overtake you, so that you become a companion of Shaytan."

He does not say *you will be punished*. He says *I fear* — the sentence discloses the son's heart before it describes the father's fate. Ibn Kathir supplies what the fear is grounded in: the torment is feared "because of your associating partners with Allah and your disobedience in what I am commanding you with."

The closing clause carries a bitter irony that ayah 44 has set up. Ibn Kathir's reading of "so that you become a companion of Shaytan": "there will be no one who will protect you, or help you, or assist you, except Iblis. However, neither he, nor anyone else, has any power over the outcome of matters. Following him will only cause you to be surrounded by the torment (of Allah)." So the man who spends his life obeying Shaytan ends up with Shaytan as his only patron — and that patron can do nothing for him. Ibn Kathir sets alongside it: "By Allah, We indeed sent (Messengers) to the nations before you, but Shaytan made their deeds fair seeming to them. So he is their helper today (in this world), and theirs will be a painful torment" (16:63).

Set that against "follow me, I will guide you to the straight path" two sentences earlier. What Ibrahim lays before his father is not a choice between following someone and standing alone. It is a choice between two companions, and between where each of them arrives.

## Living it

- **Lead with the question, not the verdict.** Ibrahim's first move (ayah 42) is to point at something and invite his father to realise the fallacy himself. That is what Maʿārif singles out as prophetic wisdom.
- **Say nothing that wounds the person while you are correcting the belief.** Maʿārif's observation stands on its own: not a single derogatory word that could hurt his father's feelings; *infidel* and *sinner* carefully avoided.
- **Keep the title of honour in place.** Ibrahim repeats *yā abati*, the mark of love and respect, at the head of every sentence — precisely where a lesser man would drop it.
- **Base your claim on knowledge, not on ego.** "There has come to me the knowledge" (ayah 43) — what he invokes is what was granted to him by Allah, and the invitation is to walk together.
- **Let the warning come from love.** "I fear lest a torment... should overtake you" (ayah 45) is spoken by a son who cannot bear the thought of his father's loss. Warning is not a hostile act when it is spoken like that.
- **Attend to the manner of the call.** Maʿārif's whole treatment of these ayat is framed as instruction in how to give counsel to elders — the manner is what a caller is answerable for.

## A note on what came next (beyond this passage)

Ayat 41–45 end with the fourth appeal; the father's reply belongs to ayah 46, outside this unit. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions it while commenting here, and it is worth knowing where the speech landed: even to these respectful entreaties his father paid no heed. Instead of giving thought to what was said and adopting a gentle attitude, he answered in very harsh language — where Ibrahim's loving *yā abati* should have called for a soft and tender response such as *yā bunayya* ("my dear son"), his father chose to call him by his name, "*Yā Ibrāhīm*," and not only threatened to stone him to death but also asked him to leave his house. Maʿārif adds that how Ibrahim then responded to that threat is worthy of deep reflection — and that response lies in the ayat that follow.

passages.title: Abraham disowned, and granted a righteous line
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close the account of Ibrahim in this surah. In the ayat just before, he had pleaded with his father in the tenderest possible words. Here we hear the father's answer (46), Ibrahim's reply and his withdrawal (47–48), and then what Allah gave him in exchange for everything he walked away from (49–50). One movement holds the passage together: a son loses his father for the sake of tawhid — worshipping Allah alone — and Allah gives him back a household of prophets.

## Ayah 46 — the answer he got

To feel this ayah you have to hear what came before it. Ma'arif ul Qur'an draws out how Ibrahim had spoken: he opened every sentence of his appeal with **ya abati** ("my dear father"), a word that in Arabic conveys deep respect and intense love for one's father. There is not a single derogatory word in the whole address that could hurt his father's feelings — words such as "infidel" or "sinner" are carefully avoided. Instead, guided by prophetic wisdom, he merely drew his father's attention to the helplessness and insensitivity of his idols, so that the man might himself realise the fallacy of his beliefs; then he mentioned the prophetic knowledge Allah had granted him; then he warned him against the divine wrath that infidelity and idolatry invite. Ma'arif notes what a balancing act this was: Ibrahim found his father living a life of unbelief and polytheism and calling others to follow him in it — the very things he was sent to eradicate — while at the same time feeling a son's love and respect for him. He held both together without letting go of either.

The father does not answer in kind. The loving **ya abati** should have called for a soft and tender response, such as **ya bunayya** ("my dear son"); instead he calls his son by his bare name, **ya Ibrahim**, and then threatens him and orders him out of the house.

The translation before us renders the father's words, "How dare you reject my idols, O Abraham!" Ibn Kathir renders them, **"Do you revile my gods, O Ibrahim?"** — and unpacks what the father is really saying: *if you do not want to worship them and you are not pleased with them, then at least stop cursing, abusing and reviling them.* It is the reflex of a man with no argument left. He does not defend the idols; he simply demands that they not be criticised.

**"La'arjumannaka."** Ma'arif reads the threat in its plainest sense: he threatened to stone him to death. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas, as-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj, ad-Dahhak and others that the meaning is, "For verily, if you do not cease, I will punish you, curse you and revile you" — the threat mirrors the accusation: *stop reviling my gods, or I will revile you.* Either way, violence and abuse take the place of any reply to what his son had actually said.

**"So get away from me *Maliyan*."** The commentators record two readings of that last word, both preserved with attribution:

- **"Forever," or "for a long time."** Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr and Mujahid bin Ishaq all said *Maliyan* means "forever"; al-Hasan al-Basri said "for a long time"; as-Suddi said "forever." On this reading it is a permanent expulsion: *never come back.*
- **"Go away in peace and safety before you are afflicted with a punishment from me."** Ibn 'Abbas said this, in the reports of 'Ali bin Abi Talhah and al-'Awfi, and ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, 'Atiyah al-Jadali, Malik and others said the same. **This is the view Ibn Jarir preferred.** On this one the sentence is a countdown: *get out while you still can.*

## Ayah 47 — "Peace be on you!"

Ibrahim is threatened and thrown out, and his entire answer begins with a word of peace.

Ibn Kathir places this alongside two descriptions of the believers elsewhere in the Qur'an: "and when the foolish address them (with bad words) they say, *Salaman* [peace]" (25:63), and "when they hear false speech they withdraw from it and say: 'To us our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be to you. We seek not the way of the ignorant'" (28:55). The meaning of Ibrahim's **salamun 'alayk**, he says, is: *"You will not receive any insult or harm from me."* And he adds why: **this is due to the respect and honour of fatherhood.** The father forfeited a father's decency; the son did not forfeit a son's.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an gives the word two possible senses here. The first is the one above: *salam* used to signify the severance of a relationship in a polite manner, so as not to cause hurt — a way of conveying, "though I do not agree with your views, I will not harm you," which the Qur'an describes as an attribute of good and pious people. The second is *salam* in its conventional sense of a greeting — and that raises a real question, since the Prophet ﷺ forbade the believers to be the first to greet a disbeliever with *salam* on meeting him.

Ma'arif lays the evidence out honestly. **Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim** report from Sayyidna Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said, *"Do not be the first to greet Jews and Christians with the word salam."* But **Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim** also report through Sayyidna Usamah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ greeted first a group of people among whom infidels, polytheists and Muslims were all present. This, Ma'arif explains, is the source of the differences that developed among the jurists on the question — by their words and actions, eminent Companions, their followers and leaders of religious thought expressed different views on it, and al-Qurtubi treated the subject in great detail while explaining this verse in his book *Ahkam ul-Qur'an*. Ma'arif then cites the ruling of Imam an-Nakha'i: when one meets a non-Muslim on a religious or worldly need, there is no harm in taking the lead in greeting him with *salam*, but one should avoid greeting first where there is no need to meet him. Thus, Ma'arif says, both of the Prophet's ﷺ sayings are reconciled.

## "I will ask forgiveness of my Lord for you" — and how long he kept it up

Ibn Kathir explains the promise simply: *"But, I will ask Allah to guide you and forgive you for your sin."* And he did — for a very long time. Ibn Kathir traces it: Ibrahim continued to seek forgiveness for his father even after he had migrated to Ash-Sham, even after building the Sacred Masjid in Makkah, and after the birth of his two sons Isma'il and Ishaq, as can be seen in his prayer, *"Our Lord! Forgive me and my parents, and all the believers on the Day when the reckoning will be established"* (14:41). A lifetime of quiet petitions for a man who had thrown him out.

From this tradition, in the beginning stages of Islam, the Muslims used to seek forgiveness for their relatives and family members who were polytheists, following the way of Ibrahim, the *Khalil* — the Friend of Allah — until Allah revealed, *"Indeed there has been an excellent example for you in Ibrahim and those with him, when they said to their people: 'Verily, we are free from you and whatever you worship besides Allah'"* — with the express exception, *"except the saying of Ibrahim to his father: 'Verily, I will ask forgiveness for you, but I have no power to do anything for you before Allah'"* (60:4). Ibn Kathir's gloss on that exception is exact: *except for this statement, so do not follow it.* Then came, *"It is not proper for the Prophet and those who believe to ask Allah's forgiveness for the idolators"* (9:113), and the explanation, *"And Ibrahim's invoking for his father's forgiveness was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he is an enemy of Allah, he dissociated himself from him. Verily, Ibrahim was Awwah, forbearing"* (9:114). (The rendering before us leaves the word *Awwah* untranslated, and our sources do not explain it here, so it is left as it stands.)

So the apparent problem — how could Ibrahim promise something later declared unlawful? — has a clear answer, given by both commentaries: **the promise was made before such a prayer was forbidden; the prohibition was imposed after this event.** Ma'arif adds that Ibrahim's promise was made before his father's firm adherence to infidelity and his hostility to Allah had become clearly evident; when the position was no longer in doubt, Ibrahim announced his dissociation from him. Ma'arif notes that our Prophet ﷺ passed through something of the same: he told his uncle Abu Talib that he would keep praying to Allah for his forgiveness until he was forbidden to do so — and after 9:113 was revealed, he stopped seeking forgiveness for his uncle. (Ma'arif relays these words without naming a hadith collection for them, so they are passed on here as it gives them.)

There is real tenderness in this, and a real limit. Ma'arif states the law plainly — to ask forgiveness for the sins of one who rejects faith is prohibited and unlawful in Islamic law; and note what Ibn Kathir says Ibrahim's promise actually amounted to — *"I will ask Allah to guide you and forgive you for your sin"* — a plea for his father's guidance while there was still time. When the limit came down, Ibrahim submitted to it and withdrew the promise. Yet in the very ayah that records the withdrawal, Allah calls him **halim** — forbearing — praising him in the moment of his hardest obedience. Submitting to Allah's limit is not coldness.

**"Verily, He is unto me *Hafiyya*."** Ibn 'Abbas and others said that *Hafiyyan* means **kind** — meaning, "since He guided me to worship Him and direct my religious devotion to Him alone." As-Suddi said: *al-Hafi* is the One who is concerned with his affair. Notice where Ibrahim's confidence comes from at the moment he is losing everything: not from his own standing, but from the kindness Allah had already shown him in guiding him.

## Ayah 48 — the clean break

**"And I shall turn away from you and from those whom you invoke besides Allah. And I shall call upon my Lord."** Ibn Kathir: this means, *"And I worship my Lord alone, associating no partners with Him."*

Ma'arif catches the balance precisely. On the one hand Ibrahim went to the extreme in showing respect and love for his father. On the other hand he did not allow the slightest doubt to be cast on his expression of the truth or on his total belief in it: he willingly accepted his father's order to leave the house, and he made it known that he had totally dissociated himself from those idols and addressed his prayers only to Allah. Courtesy without compromise; separation without spite.

**"And I certainly hope that I shall not be unblessed in my invocation to my Lord."** Ibn Kathir makes an important point about the word ***'Asa*** ("I hope"): here it means **that which will necessarily occur**, and not something hoped for from what is impossible. This is Ibrahim speaking — and, as Ibn Kathir says, he is the leader of the Prophets other than Muhammad ﷺ. His "I hope" is certainty spoken in the humble grammar of a servant.

Ma'arif reads this sentence as itself a prayer: beneath the expressed hope that Allah would not abandon him is a request that Allah protect him from the pain of loneliness after leaving his house and family. The next ayah describes the manner in which that prayer was granted.

## Ayat 49–50 — what Allah gave him instead

**"So when he had turned away from them and from those whom they worshipped besides Allah, We gave him Ishaq and Ya'qub, and each one of them We made a Prophet."**

Ibn Kathir states the principle in one line: when the Friend of Allah withdrew from his father and his people for the sake of Allah, **Allah gave him in exchange those who were better than them.** Ma'arif says the same: he left his father's family and was granted a better family, one consisting of prophets and pious people.

The two named are his son Ishaq and Ishaq's son Ya'qub — a son and a grandson, as Allah says elsewhere, "and Ya'qub, a grandson" (21:72) and "and after Ishaq, of Ya'qub" (11:71). Ibn Kathir notes there is no difference of opinion about Ishaq being the father of Ya'qub, and points to Surat al-Baqarah, where the sons of Ya'qub name the fathers whose Lord they will worship: "Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq" (2:133).

Why mention only these two? Ibn Kathir answers: to show that Allah made prophets from among Ibrahim's own descendants and successors, **in order to give him relief and happiness in his life.** He had lost a father; Allah gave him a son and a grandson who were prophets, and let him see it. Ibn Kathir even reasons from the wording: if Ya'qub had not become a prophet in Ibrahim's lifetime, Allah would not have limited the promise of prophethood to him, but would have mentioned his son Yusuf as well — for Yusuf too was a prophet, just as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, in a hadith Ibn Kathir describes as one whose authenticity is agreed upon, when he was asked who was the best of people: *"The Prophet of Allah, Yusuf, the son of the Prophet of Allah Ya'qub, the son of the Prophet of Allah Ishaq, the son of the Friend of Allah Ibrahim."* In another wording of this hadith: *"Verily, the noble one is the son of the noble one, who is the son of the noble one, who is the son of the noble one. That is Yusuf, the son of Ya'qub, the son of Ishaq, the son of Ibrahim."*

Ma'arif adds a quiet human detail: it was further revealed to Ibrahim that this son would have a long life and would himself beget a son by the name of Ya'qub — and the granting of a son is itself proof that Ibrahim was married by then. The lonely emigrant was told about his grandchild.

Then ayah 50: **"And We gave them of Our mercy, and We granted them *Sidqin 'Aliyyan* on the tongues."** 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn 'Abbas said *Sidqin 'Aliyyan* means **the good praise**; as-Suddi and Malik bin Anas said the same. Ibn Jarir explained why Allah said ***'Aliyyan*** — loftiness, exalted: **because all of the religions commend them and mention them with praises**, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon them all.

Set that beside ayah 46. A man was threatened in his father's house and told to get away from him. Allah answered by giving him a name that all the religions commend.

## Living it

- **Speak to elders the way Ibrahim spoke.** Ma'arif titles this passage "How to give counsel to elders," and the address in these ayat is its model: begin with honour, use no word that would wound, draw attention to the truth rather than pronounce a verdict, and let warnings come wrapped in concern.
- **Do not let being abused make you abusive.** Ibrahim answered a threat with "Peace be on you." Ibn Kathir grounds that not in weakness but in *the respect and honour of fatherhood* — a right that survived even the father's wrongdoing.
- **Separate from falsehood without separating from good character.** Ayah 48 is a total break on belief and worship, spoken without one harsh word.
- **Trust the exchange.** Ibn Kathir's sentence on ayah 49 is worth keeping: when Ibrahim withdrew from his father and his people *for the sake of Allah*, Allah gave him in exchange those who were better than them. Note the order in the ayah — the withdrawal comes first, and the gift comes after.

passages.title: Moses called from the right side of the mount

Three short ayat give a complete portrait of Musa (peace be upon him): what Allah made him, what Allah did for him on the mountain, and what Allah gave him for the road ahead. What holds them together is that Allah is the subject of every verb — *We called*, *We drew near*, *We granted*. Musa's greatness is not presented as something he achieved but as something he was given.

## Where this passage sits

Ibn Kathir points out the deliberate ordering: after Allah had mentioned Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, and commended him, He next mentioned **Al-Kalim** — which Ibn Kathir glosses as "the one spoken to by Allah directly." The sūrah moves from one form of nearness to another: the intimacy of friendship, then the intimacy of being spoken to. Ayah 51 opens with a direct instruction — *wa-dhkur fi'l-kitāb Mūsā*, "And mention in the Book, Musa," addressed, as the translation makes explicit, to the Prophet ﷺ. This is not a story told for its own sake; the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to bring it forward and set it before people.

## "He was Mukhlasan" — the word the whole passage turns on

Ayah 51 describes Musa with a single word, **مُخْلَصًا** (*Mukhlasan*), and the commentators draw out more than one sense of it.

**Purely devoted.** Ibn Kathir relates here a report of Ath-Thawri, from 'Abdul-Aziz bin Rafi', from Abu Lubabah: the Disciples of 'Isa said, "O Spirit of Allah, inform us about the one who is *Mukhlis* (purely devoted) to Allah." He answered: "That is one who does a deed solely for Allah and he does not like for the people to praise him."

Sit with that definition for a moment. It sets the bar higher than most of us imagine sincerity to be. It is not merely *not seeking* praise — it is not *wanting* it when it comes. The sincere person feels no lift when his good deed is noticed.

**Chosen.** Ibn Kathir then notes that others recited the word as *Mukhlas*, which means that he was chosen. The sense turns from active to passive: not "one who purified himself" but **one whom Allah chose**. He supports this with Allah's words to Musa elsewhere, *"Verily, I have chosen you above men"* (7:144).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the word in this second sense and renders the phrase "Indeed he was a chosen one." It explains: *Mukhlas* means a person whom Allah has chosen for Himself — someone who will not devote himself to anyone but Allah, and whose only desire is to win Allah's benevolence. This special position, the commentary says, is enjoyed by the prophets only, citing *"We purified them with a quality most pure, the remembrance of the Abode"* (38:46).

The two senses side by side say something the passage would be poorer without: sincerity is at once a striving and a gift — a deed done solely for Allah, and a person whom Allah Himself chose.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note of hope for those who are not prophets. Those among the followers of the prophets who attain perfection are also granted a place of distinction, which makes them immune to committing sins and evil deeds through Divine dispensation; they remain in Allah's protection all the time. The station itself belongs to the prophets; a share of that protective care is opened to those who follow them.

## "A Messenger, a Prophet"

Allah joins two titles for Musa in ayah 51: Messenger and Prophet. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah combined these two descriptions for him because he was one of the greatest of the Messengers, and one of the five **Messengers of Strong Will**: Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, 'Isa and Muhammad — may the blessings of Allah be upon them and upon all the Prophets.

Notice where that list sits in the sūrah's flow. Ibn Kathir observed at the outset that Ibrahim had been mentioned and commended just before this passage, and now Musa is brought forward — two of those five named in close succession, and the whole account delivered by way of a command to the last of them, the Prophet ﷺ. The reader is being shown one unbroken line of men chosen and sent.

## The mountain, and which side was "the right"

Ayah 52: **وَنَادَيْنَاهُ مِن جَانِبِ الطُّورِ الْأَيْمَنِ** — "And We called him from the right side of the Mount."

*Tur*, Ibn Kathir says, means mount. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies it as the famous mountain — Tur, or Sinai — which it describes as rising in Syria, between Madyan and Egypt, and still known by the same name; and it notes that Allah has given this mountain a distinct and special position in many ways.

Why "the **right** side"? Both commentaries answer the same way, and the answer is beautifully concrete. Ibn Kathir explains that it was on the right side **of Musa**, when he went seeking a burning wood from that fire. He saw its glow in the distance, so he set out toward it, and found it on the right side of the mountain from his own direction, at the edge of the valley that he was in. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the geography: Musa had commenced his journey from Madyan, and when he approached Tur it was on his right side.

So the Qur'an is not giving a map reference. It is describing the scene **as Musa experienced it** — a traveller down in a valley, turning toward a distant glow he could not yet explain. And this, Ibn Kathir says, is when Allah, the Exalted, spoke to him and called out to him.

Take in the contrast. He set out to fetch burning wood. He was answered by the voice of his Lord.

## "And We drew him near, in confidence"

The second half of ayah 52 — **وَقَرَّبْنَاهُ نَجِيًّا** — is the summit of the passage. Ibn Kathir: Allah summoned him to come near, and He conversed with him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word *najiyy*. The root carries the sense of a **whisper**: *munājāt* is confidential talk, and *najiyy* means a confidant — the one you take aside to speak to alone. This is the vocabulary of words shared between two, not of a public proclamation.

And note the drawing near. *Qarrabnāhu* — "We brought him close." The nearness was Allah's act, not Musa's climb. He was called, and then brought.

There is a quiet lesson in the sequence for anyone who prays. Musa did not go to the mountain to meet Allah. He went, as Ibn Kathir describes it, seeking burning wood from a fire he had seen at a distance. He was walking, and searching, and doing the small necessary thing in front of him — and it was in the middle of that ordinary errand that he was called.

## Harun: a prayer answered, and a gift

Ayah 53: **وَوَهَبْنَا لَهُ مِن رَّحْمَتِنَا أَخَاهُ هَارُونَ نَبِيًّا** — "And We granted him his brother Harun, (also) a Prophet, out of Our mercy."

Ibn Kathir explains the meaning plainly: "We responded to his request and his plea on behalf of his brother and We made him a Prophet as well." He gathers the places where the Qur'an records that plea:

- *"And my brother Harun — he is more eloquent in speech than me; so send him with me as a helper to confirm me. Verily, I fear that they will belie me"* (28:34)
- *"So send for Harun. And they have a charge of crime against me, and I fear they will kill me"* (26:13–14)
- And Allah's answer: *"You are granted your request, O Musa"* (20:36)

Look at what Musa asked for and why. He was afraid — afraid of being disbelieved, afraid of being killed for the charge held against him — and he was aware of a limitation in himself: his brother spoke more eloquently than he did. A Prophet of the highest rank, freshly spoken to by Allah, admitted his fear and asked for help. There is no shame in it. Allah recorded it in His Book without a word of rebuke.

Because of this, Ibn Kathir reports, some of the Salaf (predecessors — those who came before us) said: **"No one in this life pleaded on behalf of someone else more than Musa pleaded for his brother to be a Prophet."** The highest thing Musa could think to ask for another person was not wealth or safety, but that his brother be made a Prophet.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the verb. *Wahabnā* comes from *hibah*, whose literal meaning is **a gift** — something given freely. Musa had prayed to Allah to grant prophethood to Harun as well, in order to provide him support; the prayer was granted, and the word *wahabnā* was used to describe it — the grant of the gift of Harun to Musa. That is why, the commentary notes (citing Maẓharī), Harun (peace be upon him) is also known as **the Gift of Allah** (*hibat Allāh*).

And the gift comes **مِن رَّحْمَتِنَا** — "out of Our mercy." The brother he asked for, and the prophethood that brother received, are both filed by Allah under mercy.

## Living it

**Guard the deed from the applause.** The definition of sincerity in this passage is exacting: doing the deed solely for Allah, and not liking that people praise you for it. Test your own good deeds against it — not to despair, but to see honestly where you stand.

**Ask for others what you would want for yourself, and higher.** Musa's great request was made for someone else, and some of the Salaf singled it out as unmatched. When you raise your hands, let someone else's name be in the duʿā'.

**Say your weakness out loud to Allah.** "He is more eloquent in speech than me." "I fear they will kill me." That is how a great Prophet spoke to his Lord — plainly, without pretence — and the answer came back: *"You are granted your request, O Musa."*

**Keep walking toward the light.** Musa was on an errand when he was called. Do the small dutiful thing in front of you. Nearness, when it comes, comes as Allah's act — *We called him*, *We drew him near* — and it often finds a person mid-journey.
